Q.WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY?
A.My testimony addresses several specific aspects of the Company’s Application that relate to residential rates. My testimony also includes a discussion of the general nature of cost of service, the existence of interclass and intraclass subsidies, the overall construction of residential rate options, and the Company’s assertions regarding the purported “cost shift” associated with the monthly netting option under the Renewable and Non-renewable Resources (“RNR”) tariff (“Schedule RNR”). The specific issues that I address in my testimony are as follows:
The closure of the Residential Service Schedule (“Schedule R”) to new premises established after December 31, 2022.
The closure of the Time of Use – Residential Energy Only (“Schedule TOU-REO”) rate to additional customers effective December 31, 2022. 
The continued use of the Time of Use – Residential Demand (“Schedule TOU-RD”) as a default rate for new residential premises, which the Commission authorized in its decision in Docket No. 42516.   
The percentage-based design of the Environmental Compliance Cost Recovery Schedule (“Schedule ECCR”) as applied to coal combustion residential (“CCR”) compliance costs. 
The increase in the residential basic service charge (“BSC”) from $0.4603/day to $0.492/day.
Q.How is your testimony Organized?
A.My testimony is organized into the following sections:
Section II: I discuss the nature of cost of service, rate design, and “cost shifts” or subsidies in general, as well as in the specific contexts of Schedule ECCR and the Schedule RNR monthly netting option.
Section III: I address the collective issues associated with the availability of different residential rate options, including the Company’s proposals to close Schedule R and Schedule TOU-REO, the reasonableness of using Schedule TOU-RD as the default rate new residential premises, and the overall residential rate options framework in terms of understandability and optionality.
Section IV: I discuss the reasonableness of the proposed residential BSC and the use of the zero-intercept analysis to identify customer-related costs as it relates to setting BSCs. 
Section V: I provide closing remarks and summarized conclusions.
Q.Please summarize your recommendations to the Commission.
A.I have grouped my recommendations according to subject matter categories aligned with the sections of my testimony, as follows: 
Cost of Service and Cost Allocation – I recommend that the Commission:
Modify the manner in which CCR compliance costs are allocated to customer classes and how those costs are recovered in rates because: (a) the current percentage-based adder design of Schedule ECCR fails to reflect that CCR compliance costs are primarily energy-related, and (b) results in those costs being borne disproportionately by the residential customer class. The revised Schedule ECCR should use an energy-based allocation factor and a uniform volumetric charge design.
Pending any further information presented as part of the Company’s supplemental testimony on this issue and subsequent responses by Staff and intervenors, disregard the Company’s assertions regarding the alleged “cost shift” created by the Schedule RNR monthly netting option because the basic revenue erosion frame under which the Company presents the issue is flawed. The identification of the character, direction, and magnitude of a cost shift requires a far more extensive analysis of cost of service than the Company presents in its simplistic revenue erosion calculation. The only cost shift between Schedule RNR and non-RNR customers present in the Company’s proposed rates is an object of the Company’s own creation.
Residential Rate Options – I recommend that the Commission:
Reject the Company’s proposals to close Schedule R to new premises established after December 31, 2022 and to close Schedule TOU-REO to new customers because doing so would: (a) steer customers onto Schedule TOU-RD, which has been significantly more expensive for customers than other available rates during its tenure as the default rate for new premises, and (b) create inequities within the residential class between new and existing customers.
Eliminate the use of Schedule TOU-RD as the default rate for new premises because: (a) it has been significantly more expensive to customers than other available rates, and (b) demand rate designs in general are inferior to volumetric time of use (“TOU”) rates for providing economically efficient and consistent, actionable price signals to residential customers.
Re-designate Schedule R as the default rate for new residential premises because it is demonstrably less expensive on average compared to Schedule TOU-RD. In the alternative, should the Commission desire to retain a time-varying rate as the default rate for new residential premises, I recommend that it designate Schedule TOU-REO for this purpose. 
Pursue available options for presenting customers with clearer and more understandable information on available rate options, including but not limited to: (a) directing the rebranding the TOU-RD rate which is presently referred to as the “Smart Usage” rate by the Company, and Schedule Time of Use – Plug-In Electric Vehicle (“Schedule TOU-PEV”), which is not limited to customers with plug-in electric vehicles (“EVs”), and (b) directing GPC to develop a rates calculator tool to assist customers in selecting the rate best suited to their circumstances. 
Residential BSC – I recommend that the Commission deny the Company’s proposed increase and instead retain the current BSC because: (a) the current BSC already recovers costs in excess of the Company’s truly customer-related costs, and (b) the Company’s cost of service analysis shows a decrease rather than an increase in customer-related costs. Both of these facts, considered separately or in concert, render an increase in the BSC unjustified.  
II.Cost of Service, Cost Allocation, and Subsidies

A.Background Discussion

Q. Please describe the principle of “cost causation” in ratemaking.
A.Cost causation refers to the ratemaking principle that costs should be allocated to customers who caused those costs to be incurred. Rates that allocate the cost of providing service to a customer are generally considered fair and equitable rates.
Q. in general, HOW does Georgia Power classify costs for THE purposes of allocating costs to customers?
A.Georgia Power classifies costs as belonging to one of three categories: demand-related, energy-related, or customer-related costs. Demand-related costs are those incurred to serve peak demand. Energy-related costs are those incurred to generate electricity. Customer-related costs are those costs associated with enabling customers to receive electricity service.
Q. Please provide some examples of these cost classifications.
A.Customer-related costs are typically unrelated to a specific customer’s energy consumption. Providing a customer with a meter or preparing and sending bills are costs incurred as part of a customer being able to receive electricity service. The amount, or level, of customer-related costs is unrelated to the amount of electricity an individual customer purchases. Overall, these types of costs increase for the utility based on the number of customers as opposed to the energy usage characteristics of customers.
Demand-related costs are incurred to supply customers with their maximum, or peak, power needs. These costs are driven by the amount of energy a customer uses during one or more time increments, unlike energy-related costs which are driven by the amount of energy a customer uses over an extended span of time.
Energy-related costs are those costs the Company incurs from providing electricity to customers. These types of costs to the Company increase based on the volume of electricity the customers consume. For example, fuel is consumed to generate electricity, and the more electricity customers purchase, the more fuel is consumed, the higher the overall fuel costs. Other examples include regular equipment maintenance such as lubricating moving parts that is performed based on a set number of operating hours, or management of coal combustion residuals where combustion of some quantity of fuel results in the creation of some quantity of solid waste material. Any costs that increase in proportion to the quantity of electricity generated should be classified as energy-related costs.
Q. Is it possible to perfectly allocate costs to the customers that caused them?
A.No, for a variety of reasons. To begin with, it is impractical to directly allocate costs to individual customers, so customers are grouped into different classes such as residential, commercial, industrial, etc. That grouping alone results in imperfect cost allocation among individual customers within each class, since not all customers within a customer class are identical. A circumstance in which some customers pay costs caused by other customers is often called a “cost shift” since the burden of costs that result from some customers’ activity is effectively shifted onto other customers.
For instance, customers located in rural areas have fewer customers per mile of power line than customers in more densely populated urban areas, but both rural and urban customers of the same customer class pay the costs for all power lines allocated to that customer class. The result in this example is that customers located in densely populated areas effectively subsidize customers located in areas with less population density. Similarly, multi-family customers tend to take service from larger capacity shared infrastructure that benefits from economies of scale, making their service on a per-customer basis less costly than service for more dispersed single-family homes. Multi-family customers may also differ considerably from single-family home customers in terms of their overall usage and demand, and the patterns of their usage and demand, due to differences in electric end uses and residence characteristics (e.g., prevalence of electric heating and water heating, smaller residences, etc.).  
There are often cases where experts disagree on how costs should be classified, or the allocation methodology used to allocate costs, which can influence one’s perspective on the existence and magnitude of any cost shift present in a utility’s rates. For instance, the Company’s practice of classifying a portion of costs of the shared distribution system as customer-related using its zero-intercept analysis and allocating those costs based on the number of customers within a rate class is not accepted in many jurisdictions. Similarly, the measures of demand used to allocate production demand costs are often a source of disagreement in rates proceedings because the selection of a methodology invariably produces “winners” and “losers” and it is challenging to develop bright line tests that indicate which methodology is the most appropriate. In other words, the impacts of classification and allocation decisions play a significant role in determining the amounts of costs that a group of customers is deemed to be responsible for causing, making the question of whether a cost shift is present a matter of perspective.
Q. Please elaborate on the nature of cost shift in ratemaking.
A.To some extent cost shifts are an unavoidable consequence of the ratemaking process. Details and nuances of cost causation are inevitably blurred as a result of the aggregation, classification, grouping, and allocation that occurs with both costs and customers. The technical and interdependent nature of components in the electric system also complicates achieving a perfect allocation of costs in accordance with the principle of cost causation.
However, there are multiple types of cost shifts that we can generally describe. The previous example of a cost shift or subsidization of rural customers by urban customers could be considered an intraclass cost shift, or a cost shift that occurs between members of the same customer class. Cost shifts can also occur between different customer classes as an interclass cost shift, when, for example, residential customers are paying for costs caused by industrial customers or vice-versa.
Other types of subsidization or cost shifts exist as well. There are intertemporal (a.k.a. generational) cost shifts in which costs caused during one time period are paid by customers in a different time period, either earlier or later. Another type of cost shift is an interparty shift, where costs or risks that might otherwise be the burden of the utility or its investors are shifted onto customers.
Q. Do Georgia Power customers experience cost shifts?
A.Cost shifts of various types exist throughout the Georgia Power system. Some, such as the previously described intraclass cost shift between urban and rural customers, could be considered structural since they result from the design of the basic ratemaking process. Other cost shifts, however, are the result of more deliberate choices. 
Consider, for example, some of the cost shifts associated with the Vogtle nuclear expansion project. Current customers are charged for Nuclear Construction Cost Recovery but may or may not receive future benefits from the construction for which they are paying. This is an example of an intertemporal cost shift where costs are charged to customers in one time period but benefits are received by customers in a different time period. Ratepayers in some future time will receive the benefits of electricity from this nuclear facility, but some of the ratepayers today who have been allocated these costs will never receive the benefits of electricity from this facility.
The cost recovery for the Vogtle expansion project could also be considered an interparty cost shift. Customer financing via construction work-in-progress (“CWIP”) reduces the risk to other investors (e.g., equity and debt holders) and mitigates potential risks to the Company if the facility does not operate as expected in the future. A full pass-through of fuel costs presents a similar type of risk-shifting, as doing so places the entirety of fuel price risk on customers rather than sharing that risk between customers and a utility’s shareholders. 
Q.are you objecting to the cost recovery mechanisms used for Vogtle costs or fuel costs?
A.No, not in this testimony. I am simply pointing out that cost shifts: (a) exist in many forms, (b) can be caused by the necessity of using approximations to define cost responsibility, as well as intentional decisions, and (c) are inextricably linked to the perspective from which one views the accuracy of the mechanisms used to define cost responsibility.
B.Schedule RNR Monthly Netting and Schedule ECCR

Q. Are there other examples of potential cost shifts in Georgia Power’s rate proposal that warrant the Commission’s attention in this proceeding?
A.Yes. The Company alleges that the Schedule RNR monthly netting option creates a cost shift wherein monthly netting participants are being subsidized by non-participants. The Company has also proposed an adjustment to its proposed revenue requirement to recover a projected $1.4 million of revenue erosion which they have attributed to monthly netting compared to compensation for exports to the grid at avoided cost. This purported cost shift is the basis of the Company’s position that the Schedule RNR monthly netting option should not be expanded to allow additional customers to enroll. 
The Company also proposes to continue the current design of Schedule ECCR, which uses a percentage-based bill adder to charge customers for environmental compliance costs, the bulk of which relate to costs incurred for remediation of CCR storage sites. 
Q.Has the Company adequately demonstrated that the Schedule RNR Monthly Netting Option causes a cost shift to non-participants?
A.Understanding that the Company has been directed to file supplemental testimony on this issue, it did not do so in in its initial direct testimony for two reasons. 
First, revenue erosion should not be conflated with interclass or intraclass cost shifting. Absent the Company’s proposed revenue adjustment, any revenue erosion would be borne by the Company’s shareholders. Non-participant customers would be indifferent because their own rates would not be affected. In other words, the purported $1.4 million cost shift to non-RNR ratepayers only exists because the Company created it by making this revenue adjustment.
Second, there are two facets to any question of cost shifting: (a) the costs to serve a group of customers, and (b) what they pay for service. The Company’s revenue erosion projection addresses only one side of this equation. A complete picture is only possible with a more extensive evaluation of the long-term costs that monthly netting participants impose on the system, including the costs that they avoid for all customers or cause to be avoided for by customers within their rate class. 
Q.Is there a reason for the COmmission to give consideration to shareholder interests in regard to the projected revenue erosion?
A.No. The purported revenue erosion is one very small piece of potential variations in utility revenue, and the earnings band and sharing mechanism already adequately addresses the interests of shareholders by allowing the Company to petition for incremental cost recovery if its earned return on equity (“ROE”) falls below 9.5%. The Company does not propose any changes to this mechanism in the current proceeding. This mechanism offers a global solution to the potential for under- or over-earning with recognition that variations in earnings are inevitable. 
Carving out potential lost revenues from individual sources is counter to the purpose of the earnings band framework, which does not entitle the Company to any particular amount of revenue within the band. Stated another way, why should the Company be permitted to recover additional revenue for the benefit of shareholders if it is already earning an adequate return for those shareholders as defined by the lower boundary of the earnings band? 
Q.Please explain why you are raising Schedule ECCR design as a matter for Commission consideration as it relates to the issue of cost shifting.
A.The design of Schedule ECCR is a matter for close Commission attention because: (a) the amount of costs associated with CCR remediation is large (and will continue to grow), and (b) the present design is inconsistent with cost causation. Total proposed ECCR revenue is $937,513,791, or 10.6% of proposed overall total revenue. Schedule ECCR is not subjected to a specific cost allocation protocol for the purpose of the distributing that revenue requirement between customer classes. Rather, the allocation is effectively based on class revenues because Schedule ECCR uses a standard percentage adder to customer bills. As a consequence, Schedule ECCR effectively “enhances” every component of base rates, such as fixed customer charges, demand charges, and the different varieties of energy charges (e.g., on-peak, off-peak, individual tiers within Schedule R). This suggests that the costs being recovered via Schedule ECCR are a mix of customer-related, demand-related, and energy-related costs. However, this is not the case in practice. Rather, the bulk of costs being recovered under Rider ECCR are for CCR remediation, which is energy-related in character. 
Q.Why Should CCR remediation costs be considered energy-related rather than demand- or Customer-RElated?
 A.CCRs are produced when coal is burned as fuel. Every megawatt-hour (“MWh”) of electricity generated from the combustion of coal generates a predictable quantity of CCRs. Therefore, costs associated with CCRs are an energy-related cost and should be allocated on an energy basis. The creation of CCRs has no plausible connection to the number of customers on the system, nor does it have any relation to monthly demand peaks, maximum class demands, or levels of on-peak or off-peak energy use. The determinant of total CCR volume is total energy generated, therefore an energy allocator is appropriate. 
Q.Is there any merit to the argument that CCR impoundments are fixtures to coal-fired generation units, and therefore should be subject to the same allocation methodology as the plant itself?
A.No. The impoundment could be considered a fixture, but the CCRs themselves are not somehow tied to the plant. The very fact that in many cases CCRs must be relocated for disposal, and the costs of that relocation are directly related to the volume that must be moved, lends further support to their energy-related character. This is distinctly different from capital investments in pollution control equipment that are made in order to continue to allow a plant to operate to meet system demand and energy needs. 
Q.Should the fact that some CCR remediation costs are associated with retired plants affect the cost allocation regime?
A.No. Some amount of intergenerational cost shift will be present no matter how costs are recovered from present customers. Newer customers will always shoulder a portion of the burden of paying for the legacy costs of past users. There is no cost allocation regime that is inherently fairer for addressing this intergenerational issue. However, an energy-based allocation is fairer overall because: (a) a portion of the customer base did play a role in causing those legacy costs due to their past energy use (i.e., there has not been 100% customer turnover), and (b) not all of the Company’s coal-fired generation units are retired so CCRs that require disposal are still being produced. 
Q.how does the current allocation of CCR costs compare to an energy-based Allocation?
A. The Company’s proposed rates allocate the residential rate group 50.6% of ECCR costs, of which the bulk are CCR remediation costs, resulting in a total allocation of roughly $474.1 million to residential customers. By contrast the residential customer class accounts for only 34.3% of total system energy requirements. If an energy allocator was used in place of the present regime, residential customers would be allocated roughly $321.4 million, or approximately $152.7 million less than the Company’s proposal. The current framework that causes residential customers to bear a disproportionate share of CCR remediation costs is a clear cost shift in which residential customers are subsidizing customer classes who cause greater costs by consuming of greater amounts of energy.
Q. Have regulators in other states reached the same conclusion that CCR remediation costs are energy-related and should therefore be allocated using an energy factor?
A.Regulators in both Virginia and North Carolina determined that allocating costs associated with CCR remediation on an energy basis was consistent with the principle of cost causation. In Virginia, in a proceeding on the establishment of Dominion Energy Virginia’s Rider CCR, the Hearing Examiner found “a direct connection between the volume of CCR materials to be remediated … and the volume of fuel that was burned at the four Power Stations over many years.” Based on the established energy basis allocation of fuel-related costs and the consistency of applying “a uniform energy rate to recover all CCR remediation costs” with past fuel cost recovery “allocating …  CCR costs on an energy basis is consistent with cost causation.” Elaborating on this finding, the Hearing Examiner observed: (a) that although an energy-related allocation may result in higher costs to high-load customers those high-load customers also experienced a greater share of energy-related benefits from the combustion of coal, and (b) that allocating CCR costs on an energy basis was therefore “reasonable and equitable.” The final order from the full Virginia State Corporation Commission agreed with and adopted this finding.
In North Carolina, the North Carolina Utilities Commission (“NCUC”) likewise concluded it was appropriate to “allocate all coal ash expenditures by the energy allocation factor, rather than the demand-related production plant allocation factor.” Duke Energy Carolinas (“DEC”) had initially proposed to allocate coal ash costs on a demand basis, a position opposed by several parties. After consideration, the NCUC ultimately agreed “with Public Staff witness Maness that the amount of coal ash correlates with the amount of energy produced from coal, and that the entire DEC system benefited from that energy.” Accordingly, the NCUC ordered that coal ash costs be allocated system-wide on the energy-related factor.
Q.How do you REcommend that the Commission address the cost shift caused by the design of Schedule ECCR?
A.The Commission should direct GPC to modify Schedule ECCR to use an energy-based allocation factor to determine class revenue requirements, and to modify the rate design from a percentage-of-bill based design to a uniform volumetric charge.
III. Residential Rate Options

Q.Please Briefly Describe the Company’s proposals for revising the rate options available to residential customers.
A.The Company proposes to close two fully volumetric residential rates (Schedule R and Schedule TOU-REO) to certain residential customers after December 31, 2022. Schedule R uses a non-time-differentiated inclining block rate design during the summer (June – September) and a declining block structure during the non-summer months. Schedule TOU-REO uses a two pricing period design with an on-peak period during the summer months and a flat rate for summer off-peak and non-summer use. Schedule R would remain available to residential premises that established service prior to January 1, 2023. However, unlike Schedule R, Schedule TOU-REO would only remain available for customers already on that rate prior to January 1, 2023. With these changes, newly established residences would be left with a choice between the following rate schedules: 
Schedule TOU-RD (coined “Smart Usage”), which contains a monthly maximum demand charge applied during all months and a volumetric two-period TOU design with an on-peak period during the summer months and a flat rate for summer off-peak and non-summer use.  Schedule TOU-RD was made the default residential rate for new premises starting January 1, 2021;
Schedule TOU-PEV, (coined “Plug-In Electric Vehicle”), which is a fully volumetric whole-home TOU rate with three-period design during the summer months (on-peak off-peak, super off-peak) and a two-period design (off-peak and super off-peak) during the non-summer months. Despite its name, Schedule TOU-PEV is available to customers without electric vehicles; and 
The Pre-Pay and Flat Bill rates.  
Q.How does the Company justify its proposal for these changes to its residential rate options?
A.Company Witness Legg describes two primary objectives. First, he describes the closure of Schedule R to new premises established after December 31, 2022 as “the logical next step in the Company’s ongoing efforts to encourage residential customers to move toward more modern rate structures” and “toward more modern rate designs that send price signals that more appropriately reflect the cost of service.” Witness Legg further seems to be asserting that similar proposals from other utilities are common, stating “utilities across the country are proactively moving away from more antiquated volumetric rate designs (such as the R tariff) and toward more modern rate designs that send price signals that more appropriately reflect the cost of service.” 
With respect to Schedule TOU-REO, Witness Legg states that the proposal to close Schedule TOU-REO to new customers is motivated by a desire to “streamline the Company’s tariff portfolio and avoid customer confusion.” He further notes that GPC has two additional time-varying rate schedules that would remain available to customers (Schedule TOU-RD and Schedule TOU-PEV), and relates his view that Schedule TOU-RD rate provides “customers the most accurate price signals while providing three opportunities to save (shifting usage out of on-peak times, staggering appliance use to reduce demand, and simply using less energy).”
Q.What is your reaction to the Company’s Proposals and its Stated justifications?
A.I urge the Commission to deny the Company’s specific proposals with respect to Schedule R, Schedule TOU-REO and TOU-RD.  I fundamentally disagree with Company Witness Legg’s testimony that Schedule TOU-RD provides “the most accurate price signals” and that it provides most customers with reasonable opportunities to save money on their electric bills. As I discuss in in Section III(A) of my testimony, demand rates have considerable structural flaws that result in a misalignment with cost causation and economically inefficient price signals, in particular when they are applied to residential customers. Consequently, the Company’s apparent desire to steer customers towards Schedule TOU-RD, which started with the Company’s efforts in 2019 to designate Schedule TOU-RD as the default rate for new premises starting in 2021, rests on a weak foundation. This weak foundation is evidenced by the fact that, contrary to Witness Legg’s assertions, there is no trend in utilities moving away from volumetric rate designs in schedules available to residential customers. 
Furthermore, I object to the Company’s proposals and stated justifications for the following reasons:
The closure of Schedule R to new premises starting in January 2023 would create an undeniable inequity within the residential customer class based on the arbitrary distinction of living in a newly constructed home. 
During its tenure as the default rate for new residential premises, Schedule TOU-RD has proven to be significantly more expensive to participating customers than other available rate options, rendering further efforts to steer customers towards this rate not in the best interests of GPC’s residential customers. 
On the matter of the need to streamline the Company’s residential rate offerings in order to avoid customer confusion, I agree that there is the potential for customers to become confused about their options, and be unable to determine the rate that best suits their needs. However, I disagree that the number of options is necessarily the core problem, or that the Company’s customers’ interests would be best served by reducing rate optionality in the manner the Company proposes. Rather, part of the problem lies in the confusing manner that the Company presents those options to customers, such as Schedule TOU-RD being presented with a positive connotation as the “Smart Usage” rate, and misnamed Schedule TOU-PEV being presented as the “Plug-In EV” rate when in fact it is available to customers without EVs. Another part of the problem is a lack of tools and resources that could assist customers in selecting the rate most suitable for their needs.
Q.At several points you have stated that GPC is engaged in efforts to “steer” customers onto Schedule TOU-RD. Please elaborate on the basis for that assertion.
A.There are several actions that the Company has taken or proposes to take towards this objective, even if the rate itself remains “optional” as follows:
The use of Schedule TOU-RD as the default rate for newly constructed premises effectively ensures enrollment growth and a steady supply of new prospective participants. 
Schedule TOU-RD is branded as the Smart Usage rate on the Company’s website, which has a descriptive, positive connotation for customers seeking to manage their energy bills, and the marketing materials indicate that saving money on the rate requires only “small changes.” Both claims are highly questionable.
The Company now proposes to close the only two-period TOU rate option (Schedule TOU-REO) leaving customers that desire to take TOU service under a two-period TOU rate with one option, Schedule TOU-RD. Furthermore, the only other TOU rate option beyond Schedule TOU-RD that would be available is Schedule TOU-PEV, which is marketed as a rate for customers with Plug-In EVs. A customer without an EV reviewing the Company’s website for rate options could easily overlook Schedule TOU-PEV as an option given how it is named and marketed.
The Company now proposes to close off Schedule R to new residential premises, leaving customers principally with a choice between Schedule TOU-RD and Schedule TOU-PEV, which as noted they could only know that they qualify for by navigating to the tariff itself (which requires clicking through multiple layers on the Company’s website that emphasize that TOU-PEV is for EV owners).
A.Flaws of Demand Rates

Q.Please explain in general why demand rates are inconsistent with the principle of cost causation.
A.    Grid infrastructure costs are caused by aggregate customer contributions to peak demands on different parts and levels of the system. A customer’s monthly non-coincident maximum demand only approximates their contribution to those costs for facilities in close proximity to the customer, such as secondary service lines and line transformers. Even line transformers will experience peaks that depart from individual customer peaks if they serve multiple customers because the peak demands of individual customers often do not occur at exactly the same time. The greater the number of customers (and different types of customers) served by a given piece of infrastructure, the greater this diversity benefit becomes. 
Non-coincident demand charges fail to account for this diversity and fail to account for the time-differentiated nature of generation, transmission, and distribution capacity costs. The departure from cost causation is particularly pronounced at the generation capacity and transmission level where an enormous amount of load diversity is present, but it also exists at a significant level on the distribution system as individual distribution circuits often serve thousands of customers with different electricity usage patterns.
Q.Do the cost allocation methodologies used by the Company reflect this diversity benefit?
A.Yes. In the Company’s cost of service study, production demand costs are allocated based on class demands at the time of the 12 monthly peaks (“12CP”). Certain transmission costs are allocated based on only the monthly peaks during June – September (“Summer 4CP”) while the balance of transmission costs are also allocated according to the 12CP methodology.  
Distribution cost allocation uses a hybrid system under which a portion of distribution costs are classified as customer-related according to the Company’s minimum-intercept study and allocated based on the number of customers, and the remaining balance of costs are classified as demand-related and allocated based on non-coincident maximum class demand. This maximum class demand methodology assigns costs based on the maximum demand of a given customer class during any single hour of the year. Although maximum class demand is sometimes referred to as a “non-coincident peak” allocator because the timing of the maximum demand of a given class may not be coincident with peak conditions on the broader system, this measure of demand still has a coincident character since it measures customer demands coincident with the maximum demand of the class as a whole. This is distinctly different from how a non-coincident demand charge functions because a non-coincident demand charge is based on an individual customer’s demand at any time, regardless of whether that demand occurs during times when aggregate class demand or system demand are at their highest. 
Q.does the Demand charge Component of TOU-RD reflect the time-differentiated character of demand-related costs?
A.No. The TOU-RD demand charge is based on a customer’s maximum demand during a 60-minute interval each monthly billing period regardless of when that demand occurs. That demand may be offset from the time periods that are likely to produce a peak on the system or within the residential customer class, and by using a single hourly value, the demand charge fails to reflect the frequency of customer demands on the system during potential peak windows. Likewise, the demand charge does not reflect the summer-peaking character of the Company’s system, which drives the Company’s generation planning and is a component of the allocation methodology for transmission costs.
Q.Does the TOU-RD rate design provide a price signal that promotes efficient use of electric service?
A.No. There are two problems with the design. First, demand charges in general provide an inconsistent price signal to customers. Second, the price signal itself is not actionable for a typical residential customer.
Q.Please explain how the TOU-RD price signal is inconsistent.
A.The inconsistency in the price signal arises from the fact that the marginal cost of demand from a customer’s standpoint is highly diluted by previously registered maximum demands within a billing period. During a billing period, any demand below the amount of previous maximum demand has a zero marginal cost. Even if a customer’s maximum demand occurs during a peak window, they have no incentive to reduce their demands during future on-peak hours except as necessary to avoid exceeding a maximum demand amount registered earlier in the same billing period. Ultimately, this effect produces economically inefficient outcomes. For instance, during any given summer there are likely to be multiple heat waves with multi-day durations. An economically efficient rate design should incentivize a customer to reduce their demand as much as they can throughout the duration of peak conditions caused by these events. By contrast, demand rates progressively dilute the price signal hour by hour and day by day as a billing period progresses, and fail to account for the frequency and duration of high demands during peak periods.
Q.Doesn’t the volumetric TIME OF USE component of Schedule TOU-RD provide this type of consistenT price signal?
A.It does, but the price signal should be stronger. At the Company’s proposed rates, the fixed and demand components of Schedule TOU-RD account for roughly 82% of total rate revenue. The on-peak volumetric component accounts for only roughly 8.5% of total rate revenue. For comparison, the on-peak volumetric component of Schedule TOU-REO accounts for approximately 20.2% of rate revenue and the volumetric on-peak component of Schedule TOU-PEV accounts for roughly 20.7% of total rate revenue. 
Q.Please explain why the TOU-RD rate design does not provide an actionable price signal to customers.
A.The only way that a customer can reduce their costs under the TOU-RD rate design is to manage their electricity demand during every single hour of a monthly billing period, and ultimately do so consistently month after month. Such close attention to demand management is highly impractical for a typical residential customer, not to mention being unnecessary as a means of reducing system costs. 
Q.Can you elaborate on why it is impractical for residential customers to effectively manage their demand during all hours?
A.Yes. First, consider the summer months during which there are a total of 2,928 hours, each of which may require the customer’s attention even if that hour falls outside of a peak period. The notion that customers should just avoid using major appliances at the same time is much harder to execute than it sounds, in particular because a single instance of relative inattention (or personal need) can produce an outsized bill impact. For instance, during the summer months when an air conditioner is likely to be cycling consistently, it is next to impossible to avoid using an electric dryer during the same time period when the air conditioner is operating. The same is true for other daily necessities, such as cooking with an electric range or oven, not to mention other things like using a dishwasher, coffee maker, toaster, or electric hair dryer. Furthermore, even relatively flexible needs are not infinitely flexible due to family needs and schedules. These challenges are not limited to the summer months. During the winter months any customer with electric heating is likely to experience the same scheduling difficulties, incurring high bills and utility charges despite the fact the Company does not identify a winter period during which it desires customers to manage their electricity usage.
Q.What types of rates provide a more consistent, actionable price signal than the price signal sent by demand rates, including Schedule TOU-RD?
A.Time-differentiated volumetric rates improve the price signal to make it more consistent by effectively charging customers for their average contribution to peak conditions. This provides the customer with the same price signal during all potential peak hours, such that electricity demand during each individual on-peak hour has a meaningful marginal cost. This price signal should incent load shifting away from peak hours, not just those hours where a customer might register a demand above a previous maximum demand. The typical TOU price signal is also more actionable for customers because it presents a simple and predictable risk-reward calculation that can be readily planned around and managed using both technology adoption and behavioral changes. 
On a practical level, consider again that the summer months during which there are a total of 2,928 hours. The on-peak period applied for five hours on weekday non-holidays would comprise only 14.5-14.9% of those hours depending on whether the holidays fall on a weekday or a weekend. Clearly, managing energy use during on-peak periods is a more manageable proposition than doing so during all hours. Moreover, managing an on-peak TOU pricing period also allows the customer to focus their efforts on the highest value hours from the standpoint of reducing stress on the system. This allows a customer to employ technologies such as programmable and smart thermostats and other smart appliances or devices (e.g., managed EV chargers) in support of their efforts, and adopt consistent behavioral patterns for activities that are amenable to flexible timing (e.g., avoid using a dishwasher or an electric dryer).  
Q.Do smart Appliances realistically offer customers opportunities for customers to manage demand charges?
A.No. Smart appliances are not an effective means to manage demand charges. Smart devices are suited towards management of predictable TOU pricing windows and response to demand reduction dispatch during critical peak periods, but they do not function as a means of reducing demand during all hours of a day as is required to manage a demand charge. For example, a smart thermostat or smart EV charger can be: (a) programmed to concentrate operation during off-peak periods, and (b) respond to a demand reduction dispatch signal during critical peak periods. However, neither of these capabilities are sufficient to manage demand rate cost management because they depend on known, targeted use management periods and targeted dispatch during unpredictable critical peak periods. In fact, their use towards these ends would likely have the effect of concentrating demand during other periods (e.g., overnight low-cost periods) resulting in a higher charge to the customer, despite the fact that they are responding to a signal to reduce their consumption during on-peak periods. 
Demand rate management requires integrated, coordinated operation during all hours among these end-uses, as all other electricity end-uses present in a residence. That is not something that smart appliances themselves can manage. Such coordinated management would require an entire “smart home” system where all end-uses are controlled under an overarching objective of limiting demand at all times. Establishing an integrated smart home is highly impractical for the vast majority of residential customers, whether they reside in new premises or existing homes.
Q.Is this view of rate design and economic inefficiency shared by others?
A.Yes. The Regulatory Assistance Project (“RAP”) recently published a Policy Brief (“RAP Policy Brief”), which I have attached to my testimony as Exhibit JRB-2.  In examining the rationale for demand charges, RAP concludes that such charges have little or no place in modern rate design:
Demand charges as we’ve known them in the United States should largely become a relic of the past. Current forms of demand charges, based on 15-minute, 30-minute or 60-minute individual customer peaks and often intended to recover the lion’s share of capacity costs, are neither cost reflective nor efficient in general. For much of the 20th century, traditional demand charges may have been a second-best alternative that worked reasonably well for high-load-factor industrial customers. Developments of the past several decades have, however, made even this application of demand charges archaic. Such charges do not reflect the cost drivers of the modern electric system, and typical sizing of these charges are larger than justified by proper economic analysis of the electric system. Peak window demand charges, while an improvement over their traditional counterpart, do not solve many of the core deficiencies of demand charges as an efficient pricing mechanism. Time-varying rates, including TOU rates and critical peak pricing, are more efficient than peak window demand charges.

Q.Why do the authors of the RAP Policy Brief reach this conclusion?
A.They raise the issues that I have also raised, specifically that what matters for cost causation is not a customer’s individual peak, but their contribution to peak demands on the system (or a segment thereof), and that time-differentiated energy rates are more economically efficient than demand rates. They further observe that a significant portion of capacity investment is more properly classified as energy-related rather than exclusively demand-related because, “Put simply, not all capacity costs are incurred to meet peak demand. As a result, capacity costs for generation should either be split into the traditional demand-related and energy-related categories, or else those categories should be updated into a more modern time-based classification framework.” 
B.Modernization of Electric Rate Design

Q.Apart from GPC, Are there any other Investor-Owned Utilities (“IOUs”) in the nation that use a default rate for residential customers that includes a demand charge?
A.No. The Company is an outlier in this respect. To the extent that Company Witness Legg is implying that “antiquated volumetric rate designs” are being replaced with demand rate designs, he is incorrect. 
Q.are there any other IOUS in the Nation that have closeD traditional volumetric rate designs to newly constructed residential premises?
A.No. I am not aware of any other utility that has made a proposal of this type in recent years, let alone one that has seen such a proposal adopted. A small number of IOUs have made proposals to establish a demand rate component within the standard residential rate, but none of those proposals have been adopted. There are no other IOUs in the country that either: (a) use rates with demand charge components as default rates for new or existing residential premises, or (b) otherwise apply them in a mandatory fashion in residential rates.
Q.What would be a more accurate characterization of trends in residential rate modernization?
A.Generally, the trend is towards greater availability of different rate options for the residential class, with an emphasis on making time-varying rates available as an additional option to flat or tiered rates. To be sure, the availability of different rate options has often included new optional demand rates, often with a time-varying element, in addition to volumetric TOU rates. However, there is no trend towards migrating residential customers to demand rates as GPC is seeking to do by using a demand rate as the default rate for new premises and closing other volumetric rate options. Any assertion that such a trend exists is simply inaccurate.
Where time-varying rates have been adopted as default rates, such as in California, Colorado and Michigan, volumetric TOU rates (not demand rates) have been selected as the default rate. Furthermore, customers in those jurisdictions typically have access to one or more additional volumetric TOU rates beyond the default rate. Most commonly, movement towards TOU pricing for residential customers is to offer at least one relatively “simple” option (e.g., a two-period TOU rate) and at least one more complex option. TOU rates used as default rates tend towards the simple option with other features such as a limited on-peak, off-peak rate spread that help limit customer bill impacts. 
Q.are there any examples of regulators responding to concerns about the impact that demand rates can have on some customers and their alignment with cost causation?
A.Yes. In Colorado, regulators recently ordered Black Hills Energy (“BHE”) and Xcel Energy Colorado (“Xcel CO”) to increase the availability of non-demand rates to small commercial customers. BHE was ordered to expand the eligibility for non-demand rate service to small commercial customers increasing by the maximum customer demand threshold for non-demand rates for small commercial customers from 10 kW to 50 kW. Likewise, in 2021 Xcel CO was directed to increase the maximum customer demand eligibility threshold for its small commercial non-demand rate schedule from 25 kW to 50 kW. 
In the same decision, the Colorado Public Utilities Commission (“COPUC”) also required Xcel CO to offer a pilot rate for secondary voltage general service customers (“SG-TOU Pilot”) that uses a primarily volumetric TOU-based rate design with a modest demand charge limited to secondary distribution costs. In establishing the SG-TOU Pilot, the COPUC found that there was insufficient evidence to make a broad determination on the virtues of a holistic shift away from demand rates in the proceeding, but noted significant concerns surrounding the cost causation attributes of demand rates, as follows:
However, we do find the evidence and arguments in the record of this Proceeding demonstrate a clear need for further examination of the merits of developing an alternative approach to rates for the SG customer class that better reflects actual cost causation and the Commission’s energy policy priorities. In particular, we recognize that COSSA/SEIA has raised significant and timely issues related to demand rates that warrant a much closer look in the Company’s next Phase II rate case. Those issues include, without limitation, the relationship of non-coincident demand charges to cost causation, and how the Commission should view rates that rely heavily on the demand component for recovery in light of: (a) the broad move to time differentiated rates for other major rate classes in an effort to send more accurate price signals; and (b) the potential risk that the current design may be at odds with state policy goals related to both solar adoption, as well as electrification of smaller commercial facilities. [Emphasis added.]

Beyond this example, in April 2020 the Delaware Public Service Commission (“DEPSC”) ordered Delmarva Power (the state’s only IOU) to notify all of their commercial customers of their eligibility for non-demand rates in response to petition from the Delaware Division of the Public Advocate (“DEDPA”). The issue arose due to Delmarva Power’s implementation of the customer demand cap in the non-demand small general service rate, which over time resulted in many customers being involuntarily switched to the medium general service rate, which uses a demand-based rate design. After registering demands below the threshold during the following year, customers that were switched to demand rate were not being switched back to the non-demand rate, or being notified of their eligibility to do so, resulting in many remaining on a rate that was more expensive for them. At the time it was estimated that roughly 5,000 of Delmarva Power’s 13,700 medium general service customers (36.5%) qualified for the non-demand small general service rate.
Q.How are the examples in Colorado and Delaware Relevant to residential Demand rates given that they all relate to non-residential rates?
A.The use of demand rates in rate designs for non-residential customers has historically been common, in particular for larger customers, but the same is not true for residential rates. This is in part because the prevalence of high load factor customers who benefit from demand rate designs tends to increase with demand. In other words, many non-residential customers subject to demand rates are accepting of them because the rate design costs them less than a volumetric rate would. At the same time, demand rates applied to high load factor customers may have a somewhat better alignment with cost causation because relatively constant demands tend to make an approximation to a customer’s contribution to peak demands based on a monthly maximum demand measurement somewhat more accurate.
Residential customers in general are highly dissimilar to the types of high load factor customers for whom demand rates are beneficial and for whom cost causation may be fairly well-aligned (even if only incidentally). The Delaware and Colorado examples highlight the fact that, like most residential customers, not all small commercial customers fit this profile, and for those customers demand rates can be punitive and inconsistent with cost causation. 
Q.CAN YOU PROVIDE ANY EXAMPLES OF REGULATORS REDUCING THE ROLE THAT DEMAND RATES PLAY IN THE RESIDENTIAL RATE CONTEXT?
 A.No, because demand rates are not currently deployed as default or standard residential rates by any IOU in the country. As previously noted, none of the small number of utility proposals in recent years to introduce demand charges into standard or default residential rates have been adopted, so there is no role that demand rates play in residential rate design that could be reduced or eliminated.
 Q.are there any Other indications of movement towards greater availability of non-demand rates to different types of customers?
A.Yes. There is a prominent trend is taking place in the context of rates charged for non-residential EV charging. Numerous utilities throughout the country now offer rates that allow volumetric charges to be substituted for demand charges, or establish limits or caps on demand charges for high capacity EV charging stations, in particular public direct current fast charger (“DCFC”) stations. GPC is proposing one such rate in the current proceeding in the form of Schedule Charge It-Electric Vehicle (“CIEV”). Although this trend is associated with a specific challenge faced by high capacity EV charging, at its core it acknowledges the fact that demand charges can be punitive to customers with low load factors. 
C.The Schedule TOU-RD Default Rate Experience 

Q.Please describe how Schedule TOU-RD came to be deployed as a Default Rate for new residential premises.
A.In the Company’s 2019 rate case, it proposed to make Schedule R unavailable to new residential premises beginning in January 2020. The Settlement Agreement adopted in the 2019 rate case did not adopt this proposal, but did allow the Company to use Schedule TOU-RD as the default rate for new residential premises starting in January 2021. This means that new customers are placed on Schedule TOU-RD unless they opt into another rate option when they begin service.  The Settlement also obligated the Company to “report back to the Commission at the time of its next base rate case regarding the adoption of TOU-RD and its use as the default rate for newly constructed residential premises.”   
Q.How is the customer rate election, or opt-Out option, actually implemented?
A.The mechanics, such as how a customer specifically is presented with the choice of rates, how they are notified that they have a choice in rates, and how the merits and drawbacks of different rate options are explained to customers are not very clear. For instance, the Schedule R and Schedule TOU-RD tariffs and webpages contain no mention that Schedule TOU-RD is the default rate for new residential premises. Likewise, the materials that the Company provides to customers of new residential premises related to the default rate contain no apparent mention of other rate options, considerations that should be made when selecting a rate, or guidance on how to execute a rate election at the time service is being requested, or a rate switch at a later date. The Company appears to provide the same materials to customers that pro-actively select Schedule TOU-RD as it does to those that reside in newly constructed premises. Exhibit JRB-3 contains the Company’s response to a Staff data request for this information, which includes a welcome letter and an example of a seasonally sent postcard.
It is possible that further information is provided to customers beginning service at a new premises via customer service agents or through others means, but if so the Company failed to clearly articulate this in written direct testimony, did not include the information in the above noted response or other responses to data requests, and failed to describe its approach to customer engagement with any specificity under cross examination.
Q.Has the Company filed any report with the Commission on its experience with the adoption of Schedule TOU-RD as the default rate for newly constructed Residential premises?
A.To the best of my knowledge there is no such formal report, or any evaluation whatsoever on the experience, lessons learned, improvements made, etc. The Company has responded to various data requests posed by Commission Staff, such as providing statistics on new enrollments and opt-outs, but as far as I can tell it has not conducted any research or analysis on its own initiative. I am not aware of any publicly filed report to the Commission that the Company has conducted in line with the provisions of the 2019 Settlement Agreement. 
Witness Legg testified that, at least since before 2019, the Company has not conducted any specific analysis of whether new customers defaulted to TOU-RD have different usage patterns, load, or cost profiles that might differ from customers taking service under other residential rate options. Likewise, Mr. Legg testified that the Company has not studied whether customers that have been on the TOU-RD tariff for at least one year have changed their behavior in response to price signals, or whether customers on the TOU-RD tariff have meaningfully different peak demand than residential customers at large.  
Q.What has been the experience of customers enrolled on Schedule TOU-RD under its use as a default rate for new residential premises?
A.Customers on the TOU-RD rate paid more than they otherwise would have for electricity under another available rate. Figure 1 shows a comparison of monthly average bills from June 2021 to May 2022 for customers enrolled on Schedule TOU-RD versus what their bill would have been if they were enrolled on Schedule R. The average TOU-RD bill over this year was $15.98/month higher than it would have been under Schedule R, totaling roughly $192 over the course of this 12-month period. 
Figure 1


Figure 1 is simply a graphical representation of data provided by the Company in response to a data request. Figures 2 and 3 show comparisons from January 2021 to June 2022 between different rate schedules based on different data sets and my own calculations of “shadow” bills under other rate schedules for the Schedule TOU-RD median customer. They also illustrate that Schedule TOU-RD is considerably more expensive for the typical customer than other available residential rate schedules. 
Figure 2 shows a monthly shadow bill comparison between Schedules R, TOU-REO, TOU-RD using the demand and energy usage from the median Schedule TOU-RD customer while Figure 3 translates these amounts into average monthly volumetric rates. 
Figure 2
 

Figure 3
 

Figure 4 shows the monthly average rate (total bill divided by usage) paid by the class median customer for each of Schedules R, TOU-PEV, TOU-REO, and TOU-RD. Like Figure 3, Figure 4 illustrates that Schedule TOU-RD is an outlier in terms of the average rate it charges customers stated in volumetric terms, in particular during the non-summer months. The difference is significant. On an annual basis the TOU-RD rate is roughly 4.8 cents/kWh higher than the average of the other rates, while during non-summer months the difference increases to roughly 5.6 cents/kWh. The difference between Figure 3 and Figure 4 is that Figure 3 shows the rate the median Schedule TOU-RD customer would have paid under other available rates, while Figure 4 shows the average rate actually paid by the median customer on each of those rate schedules.
