Even well-designed TOU rates do not necessarily reflect critical peak times very well. For
example, a four-hour weekday on-peak window for only the highest demand months will
include around 200-400 hours annually. These will necessarily contain some days with
higher peaks than others and only a limited number of hours that define utility capacity
needs for reliability purposes at peak. Simple TOU rates do not distinguish in this regard
between the moderate peaks (e.g., ordinary days in the summer) and the very highest
peaks (e.g., extremely hot days in the summer). In short, the implication is that simple
TOU rates do not provide a sharp enough incentive on actual peak days.51 In any case, we
are no longer bound to simple TOU pricing. Dynamic rates, including critical peak pricing,
peak-time rebates, variable peak pricing and real-time pricing, all better address peaking
issues because they provide higher marginal prices at the times of maximum system stress.
By concentrating customer attention on the hours that actually drive costs, the more
dynamic rates produce better results for the electric system and society.

By its very nature, a demand charge cannot present symmetric and consistent marginal
incentives in the same way as a time-varying kWh charge. Compared to traditional
demand charges, properly sized peak window demand charges have a better cost causation

kWh rates. Given the rate design possibilities that AMI offers, what reason is there to
retain demand charges at all?

4. What Might Be Left for Demand
Charges?
The foregoing demonstrates that the typical argument for demand charges, as used for
generation, transmission and shared distribution capacity, is substantially flawed. Even so,
we want to investigate if there are any circumstances, however limited, for which demand
charges are an efficient rate design.

Some theorists have identified a different and, in our minds, much narrower set of
rationales for demand charges. The case for time-varying rates relies substantially on the
diversity of load and the lack of a direct relationship between individual customer peaks
and the system peaks that drive costs. A diverse set of customers may, in the aggregate,
create a predictable load profile much of the time. But what if this diversity goes away in
an unpredictable manner? Or, for that matter, in a predictable one? Is there something
about the causation of costs in special and limited circumstances that warrants charging
for peak incurrences of short-term (e.g., 15-minute) demand for individual customers?
To answer this question, we consider three cases that, on their faces, might present a
marginal-cost justification for demand charges. The first is one that we have carved out
from the beginning: capacity costs that are not shared, such as dedicated transformers and
service drops, which we term “dedicated site infrastructure.”53 This illustrates some
important issues relevant to any broader theoretical case for demand charges. The second
is the cost associated with uncertainty in customer behavior. The third is timer peaks, a
phenomenon where customers shift usage in response to hours with lower prices.

capacity to provide their standby service. This was certainly an improvement on monthly demand charges for such customers, but, in light of

4.1 Dedicated Site Infrastructure
Dedicated transformers and service drops for individual customers are, by definition, not
shared infrastructure. The relative importance of this category of cost will vary by
customer class. Larger commercial and industrial customer classes, as long as they are
taking secondary voltage service, will often have dedicated transformers for each customer
or a dedicated transformer bank for customers taking three-phase power. Dedicated
transformers will be rare for residential customers in urban and suburban areas, but
single-family homes will almost always have a dedicated service drop. The largest
industrial customers may have their own primary line (effectively serving as a dedicated
service drop) or a dedicated substation (effectively serving as a dedicated transformer).
In rural areas, each customer will typically have a dedicated transformer, at which point
transformers are customer-specific site infrastructure.

For these customer-specific site infrastructure costs, there is no diversity of demand
between the customer meter and point of connection with the shared system. As a result,
individual customer NCPs are certainly relevant to the sizing of these components. One
might conclude from this that a demand charge can provide a reasonable pricing incentive
here. The time period for such a demand charge should have nothing to do with a shared
peak since there is no sharing of the infrastructure. Nor should it be limited to peak
windows since the peak for an individual customer could occur at any time. The cost of
these components may be no more than about $1/kW/month, a fraction of typical demand
charges.54

There are also other ways of efficiently pricing this category of costs. A similar set of
customer incentives may be presented by a connected load charge for a set amount of local
capacity. Such a connected load charge can help with efficient sizing, but only if it’s
accompanied by a fee for overages or the automatic tripping of circuits when demand
would cause an overage. Even then, a connected load charge provides no incentive for
customers to manage their usage efficiently; that is, there are no cost savings to be gained
by keeping their demand below the level of the predetermined connected load. A charge
that establishes the relationship of the customer’s individual peak demand to the sizing of
these components might, however, give the customer some incentive to minimize peaks.

It is worth examining this issue at the level of engineering and planning. What type of
customer behavior would minimize the risk of transformer overload and degradation?
Or what type of customer behavior would allow utilities to size dedicated transformers
more efficiently?

Capacity ratings for the different elements of the electric system are set with many

a sustained, multihour overload.

4.2 Risks of Customer Variance at Peak Times

unpredictable. Predictable changes often occur around the weather, one of the few
variables that simultaneously affects all customers in a given area. Regarding
unpredictable changes, consider a simple hypothetical illustrated in Figure 8.

This simple example is the essence of the argument made by Michael Veall.60 He
demonstrates that, for a given level of average customer demand during a peak, higher
variance customers lead to a risk of higher peaks, particularly if they are correlated. This,
in turn, results in a need for higher capacity planning margins. Veall constructs a detailed
economic model of optimal peak period pricing. He states that the traditional monthly
demand charge does not reasonably address this issue, but rather a peak window demand
charge can serve as marginal price on a customer’s variance. He notes additional caveats:
“If there are many small users with uncorrelated demands, the effects of an individual
user’s variation on total system variation will be small. But if users are large or their
demands are correlated, variance charges are important.”61 Finally, Veall’s result
demonstrates that, if a peak window demand charge is to be imposed, it should be paired
with an on-peak kWh rate.62 The logic around risk and Veall’s theoretical model present an
argument for a peak window demand charge that is substantially different from those that
utilities put forward. And again, we see a more defensible justification for peak window
demand charges for larger-volume customers. But the key question of correlations and
levels of risk has been neglected in the discussion around demand charges and is only a
theoretical possibility in Veall’s model. Furthermore, Veall’s model does not consider the
possibility of more granularly dynamic time-varying kWh rates.

Marcel Boiteux, the influential French economist and executive for Électricité de France
(EdF), does discuss risk and uncertainty in a 1952 paper, written jointly with his colleague
Paul Stasi.63 When it comes time for tariff design, Boiteux and Stasi describe two different
zones of the shared electric system: (1) the “collective network” and (2) the “semi-
individual network, whose capacity depends particularly on the uncertainties of
consumption of each customer.”64 With respect to the collective network, they find that the
“uncertainties of individual consumption” are small enough to be ignored.65 And, finally,
their analysis of the “semi-individual network” is dominated by risk and the irregularities
of individual customer’s loads. This leads them to a justification for a complex system of
subscription-based contract demand charges, with higher prices for contracted demand in

Based on these considerations, Boiteux and Stasi largely describe the generation and

(15-60 kV) as the “semi-individual” network.67 They are discussing these issues in the
context of the then-new Tarif Vert for high voltage industrial customers, and the
discussion could be read in a manner that is limited to those customers. This could mean
that the dividing line for the semi-individual network could vary by the size of customer.
Whether residential customer fluctuations are correlated in a significant and pertinent
way is another empirical question Boiteux and Stasi do not address. It is unclear whether
the irregularities of individual residential customers would ever be significant enough to
matter at a level higher than a shared transformer.

4.3 Timer Peaks
Michael A. Crew and Paul R. Kleindorfer (1979) raise another area where a demand charge
could theoretically be efficient, which they describe as the secondary preferences of
customers, given the structure of time-varying rates, and the shifting of demand to
notionally off-peak times. This is colloquially known as a timer peak. This occurs if
customers increase their usage substantially during hours with low rates or more
specifically right at the time when low-priced hours begin.68 In the worst-case scenario,
TOU rates can theoretically just shift the system peak without reducing it if enough usage
is shifted to hours with low prices. The same is true of coincident peak window demand
charges. This outcome can be avoided by managing the number of periods in the rate, the
hours covered by each period and the relative prices. One utility has designed a TOU rate
in which each customer chooses a three-hour peak period of 4-7 p.m., 5-8 p.m. or 6-9 p.m.
All of these customers have 6-7 p.m. in their peak period; two-thirds of them have 5-6 p.m.
and 7-8 p.m. in their peak period; and one-third have either 4-5 p.m. or 8-9 p.m. in their

66

peak period. This provides the utilities with the most powerful pricing signal during the
most likely peak hour but substantial peak reduction in the adjacent hours.69 Another
simple solution is to apply different hours to different classes or subclasses. For example,
single-family residences may have their tariff shifted one hour earlier than apartments, or
secondary general service one hour later than primary general service.

If the more general system peaks are not impacted significantly enough by this
phenomenon to warrant changing the structure of the rate, more granular and local issues
can theoretically arise. Figure 9 shows a set of results from a San Diego Gas and Electric
rate for electric vehicles, where the “super off-peak” rate begins at midnight.70


Figure 9. Real-world illustration of timer peak with EV charging on TOU rate


                      Source: Jones, B., Vermeer, G., Voellmann, K., & Allen, P. (2017). Accelerating the Electric Vehicle Market


This is a rational customer response to a TOU rate, at least for specific end uses. If an
electric vehicle is parked at home in the evening and will not be used again until morning,
then the customer has a significant amount of flexibility to choose when charging will
begin. The very beginning of the lowest price period is an obvious time to start charging.
While this may not present an issue at the generation and transmission level, assuming
midnight remains an off-peak period, bunching of EV charging could lead to issues at the
more local level.

Again, thinking about a line transformer helps focus the analysis. If five single-family
homes are served by one shared transformer and all five of those homes have EVs that
start charging at midnight, then impacts at the line transformer level are a possibility.
Furthermore, what if those houses have other timed usage that starts at the beginning of
the lowest price period? Sending a secondary price signal that discourages households


69
     Salt River Project. (n.d.). SRP EZ-3 price plan. https://www.srpnet.com/prices/home/ez3.aspx
70
     Jones, B., Vermeer, G., Voellmann, K., & Allen, P. (2017). Accelerating the electric vehicle market, p. 16. M.J. Bradley & Associates.
https://www.mjbradley.com/sites/default/files/MJBA_Accelerating_the_Electric_Vehicle_Market_FINAL.pdf


                                            Justin Barnes Direct Testimony, on behalf of GIPL
                                                        GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                      Exhibit JRB-2 | Page 38 of 42

38      |   DEMAND CHARGES: WHAT ARE THEY GOOD FOR?                                                 REGULATORY ASSISTANCE PROJECT (RAP)®


from turning on all of their major end uses at midnight could be effective. A daily-as-used
demand charge can send such a signal if it were applied across 24-hour periods. A more
traditional monthly demand charge, however, will send that signal in a much more
attenuated way. A connected load charge based on a contract demand for the cost of
connection, with fees for overages, similar to the Électricité de France Tempo rate for
residential customers,71 would send a similar price signal as well.

There are other ways to deal with this phenomenon besides price signals with demand-
charge features. The beginning of the off-peak period with the lowest price could be
staggered for different customers, for example, beginning at 10 p.m. for one-third of
customers, midnight for another third and 2 a.m. for the last third. For customers with
long-duration controlled loads, like water heaters or electric vehicles, this would be easy
for the customer to manage and beneficial to the utility. To maximize the benefits of such
an approach, one would need to have a relatively even split among those three options for
the customers on each shared transformer. Load management programs and smart
devices could deal with this type of issue as well. For some loads, particularly water
heating and EV charging, we anticipate advanced devices that will enable the utility to
manage loads to minimize costs and enable customers to benefit from even lower off-peak
rates for enabled devices.

One could even question how much of a problem this poses to the longevity of the shared
transformers in question. The ambient temperature has almost always cooled off by
midnight, and several hours of low or moderate loads could allow the transformer to cool
from significant levels of usage during the day or early evening. In certain circumstances,
it could be more convenient and cost-effective to upgrade any potentially affected
transformers, particularly where multiple water heaters or EV chargers are served from a
single transformer.


5. Conclusion
Demand charges, of either the traditional monthly NCP or peak window variety, are not
efficient, as a general matter, for shared system capacity costs because:

•       For the vast majority of customers, any peak reduction signal in a traditional monthly
        demand charge is weak and inaccurate.

•       Traditional calculations for demand charges have included far too many costs as
        demand-related. Ideally, utility commissions will adopt a new time-based classification


71
     Electricite de France. (n.d.). Tarif Bleu: Regulated sale tariff for electricity. https://particulier.edf.fr/en/home/energy-and-
services/electricity/tarif-bleu.html


                                               Justin Barnes Direct Testimony, on behalf of GIPL
                                                           GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                         Exhibit JRB-2 | Page 39 of 42

REGULATORY ASSISTANCE PROJECT (RAP)®                                              DEMAND CHARGES: WHAT ARE THEY GOOD FOR? |   39


        and allocation framework for generation, transmission and shared distribution costs.72
        Failing that, the numerous energy benefits from capacity investments should be
        properly accounted for — that is, reflected in energy, not demand, charges.

•       Simple TOU rates are superior to peak window demand charges in their own right, but
        AMI enables time-varying energy charges, such as critical peak pricing, peak-time
        rebates and variable peak pricing, that much more accurately target times of system
        stress and reward end users for shifting their loads to off-peak times.

Although we have shown the significant downsides to using current forms of demand
charges, in very limited circumstances there might be cost- and efficiency-related
justifications for certain types of demand charges. But such charges would be significantly
lower than those prevailing for industrial customers in the United States today. Dedicated
site infrastructure is a small portion of utility system costs, and typical demand charges
would not necessarily provide an optimal signal to control these costs. The primary
concerns around timer peaks are almost certainly limited to local infrastructure.

As for the general risk of customer variance and correlation, little work has been done to
investigate the statistical bases of this more sophisticated case for demand charges. We
think that it is unlikely that such an analysis would find that a substantial demand charge
would be fairer or more efficient than time-varying energy charges. Lastly, there is a better
case for demand charge-like structures for large customers, who are more likely to have
significant dedicated site infrastructure. One might also argue that high variance at peak
times among these customers has a more significant chance of influencing the overall
system peak. Any such demand charges may not look like Hopkinson rates and would
likely be only a second-best solution to a sophisticated system of time-varying energy
charges.

The economic and regulatory principles that underlie these judgments are not new. The
inescapable essentials of microeconomic theory are at work here. Boiteux, Bonbright and
Kahn follow these principles and theories, as do the other scholars and practitioners we
cite. In 1964, Paul Garfield and Wallace Lovejoy73 also stepped into the fray. They
converted principles of economic efficiency and fairness into straightforward criteria for
assessing the merits of cost allocation methods and rate designs for generation and
delivery capacity costs:

•       All utility customers should contribute to capacity costs.

•       The longer the period of time that customers preempt others’ use of capacity, the more
        they should pay for the use of that capacity.


72
     Lazar et al., 2020.
73
     Criteria adapted from Garfield, P., & Lovejoy, W. (1964). Public utility economics, pp. 163-165. Prentice Hall.


                                             Justin Barnes Direct Testimony, on behalf of GIPL
                                                         GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                       Exhibit JRB-2 | Page 40 of 42

40   |   DEMAND CHARGES: WHAT ARE THEY GOOD FOR?                         REGULATORY ASSISTANCE PROJECT (RAP)®


•    Any service that makes exclusive use of a portion of capacity should be assigned all of
     the costs for that portion of capacity.

•    The allocation of capacity costs should change gradually with changes in the pattern of
     usage.

•    More capacity costs should be allocated to on-peak usage than off-peak.

•    Interruptible service (or other forms of utility restrictions and control) should be
     allocated less in capacity costs as the degree of restriction increases.

Only time-varying energy charges can meet all of these objectives simultaneously. Demand
charges for shared costs are demonstrably less efficient and less equitable than they.

Question:

Please provide informational materials provided to customers of new residential premises related
to the default rate (TOU-RD).

Response:

New customers to the Smart Usage rate (TOU-RD) receive a welcome letter that confirms their
enrollment and provides helpful information to educate them on how to take advantage of the rate’s
design. This information is provided to all customers who enroll in the rate – regardless of whether
they reside at a newly established premises or at an existing premises. This information is provided
via email if an email address is available; otherwise, it is provided by direct mail.

Additionally, customers enrolled in Smart Usage receive multiple seasonal postcards that highlight
the on and off-peak pricing differences. The message includes specific reminders to shift usage to
capitalize on the TOU design as well as emphasizing the importance of managing demand.

The materials provided also encourage customers to visit the Georgia Power website for more
information on the Smart Usage rate and for tips on managing their energy usage.

Examples of the welcome letter and postcard communications are provided in STF-PIA-2-3
Attachment A and STF-PIA-2-3 Attachment B, respectively.

 1           II.     COST OF SERVICE, COST ALLOCATION, AND SUBSIDIES

 2                                  A.     Background Discussion

 3   Q.   PLEASE       DESCRIBE          THE   PRINCIPLE       OF    “COST      CAUSATION”          IN

 4        RATEMAKING.

 5   A.   Cost causation refers to the ratemaking principle that costs should be allocated to customers

 6        who caused those costs to be incurred. Rates that allocate the cost of providing service to

 7        a customer are generally considered fair and equitable rates.

 8   Q.   IN GENERAL, HOW DOES GEORGIA POWER CLASSIFY COSTS FOR THE

 9        PURPOSES OF ALLOCATING COSTS TO CUSTOMERS?

10   A.   Georgia Power classifies costs as belonging to one of three categories: demand-related,

11        energy-related, or customer-related costs. Demand-related costs are those incurred to serve

12        peak demand. Energy-related costs are those incurred to generate electricity. Customer-

13        related costs are those costs associated with enabling customers to receive electricity

14        service.

15   Q.   PLEASE PROVIDE SOME EXAMPLES OF THESE COST CLASSIFICATIONS.

16   A.   Customer-related costs are typically unrelated to a specific customer’s energy

17        consumption. Providing a customer with a meter or preparing and sending bills are costs

18        incurred as part of a customer being able to receive electricity service. The amount, or

19        level, of customer-related costs is unrelated to the amount of electricity an individual

20        customer purchases. Overall, these types of costs increase for the utility based on the

21        number of customers as opposed to the energy usage characteristics of customers.

22                 Demand-related costs are incurred to supply customers with their maximum, or

23        peak, power needs. These costs are driven by the amount of energy a customer uses during


                            Justin Barnes Direct Testimony, on behalf of GIPL
                                        GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                  Page 7

1         one or more time increments, unlike energy-related costs which are driven by the amount

2         of energy a customer uses over an extended span of time.

 3                 Energy-related costs are those costs the Company incurs from providing electricity

 4        to customers. These types of costs to the Company increase based on the volume of

 5        electricity the customers consume. For example, fuel is consumed to generate electricity,

 6        and the more electricity customers purchase, the more fuel is consumed, the higher the

 7        overall fuel costs. Other examples include regular equipment maintenance such as

 8        lubricating moving parts that is performed based on a set number of operating hours, or

 9        management of coal combustion residuals where combustion of some quantity of fuel

10        results in the creation of some quantity of solid waste material. Any costs that increase in

11        proportion to the quantity of electricity generated should be classified as energy-related

12        costs.

13   Q.   IS IT POSSIBLE TO PERFECTLY ALLOCATE COSTS TO THE CUSTOMERS

14        THAT CAUSED THEM?

15   A.   No, for a variety of reasons. To begin with, it is impractical to directly allocate costs to

16        individual customers, so customers are grouped into different classes such as residential,

17        commercial, industrial, etc. That grouping alone results in imperfect cost allocation among

18        individual customers within each class, since not all customers within a customer class are

19        identical. A circumstance in which some customers pay costs caused by other customers is

20        often called a “cost shift” since the burden of costs that result from some customers’

21        activity is effectively shifted onto other customers.

22                 For instance, customers located in rural areas have fewer customers per mile of

23        power line than customers in more densely populated urban areas, but both rural and urban


                             Justin Barnes Direct Testimony, on behalf of GIPL
                                         GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                   Page 8

 1            customers of the same customer class pay the costs for all power lines allocated to that

 2            customer class. The result in this example is that customers located in densely populated

 3            areas effectively subsidize customers located in areas with less population density.

 4            Similarly, multi-family customers tend to take service from larger capacity shared

 5            infrastructure that benefits from economies of scale, making their service on a per-customer

 6            basis less costly than service for more dispersed single-family homes. Multi-family

 7            customers may also differ considerably from single-family home customers in terms of

 8            their overall usage and demand, and the patterns of their usage and demand, due to

 9            differences in electric end uses and residence characteristics (e.g., prevalence of electric

10            heating and water heating, smaller residences, etc.).

11                     There are often cases where experts disagree on how costs should be classified, or

12            the allocation methodology used to allocate costs, which can influence one’s perspective

13            on the existence and magnitude of any cost shift present in a utility’s rates. For instance,

14            the Company’s practice of classifying a portion of costs of the shared distribution system

15            as customer-related using its zero-intercept analysis and allocating those costs based on the

16            number of customers within a rate class is not accepted in many jurisdictions. 3 Similarly,

17            the measures of demand used to allocate production demand costs are often a source of

18            disagreement in rates proceedings because the selection of a methodology invariably

19            produces “winners” and “losers” and it is challenging to develop bright line tests that

20            indicate which methodology is the most appropriate. In other words, the impacts of


     3
       Because this methodology allocates a larger amount of costs to highly populated classes like the residential class, it
     results in the residential class producing a lower return (i.e., below “parity”) and appearance that the residential class
     is being subsidized by other rate classes. Eliminating this element of the Company’s cost of service study would
     result in the residential class showing a higher return and classes composed of larger non-residential customers
     showing lower returns.

                                    Justin Barnes Direct Testimony, on behalf of GIPL
                                                GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                          Page 9

 1        classification and allocation decisions play a significant role in determining the amounts of

 2        costs that a group of customers is deemed to be responsible for causing, making the

 3        question of whether a cost shift is present a matter of perspective.

 4   Q.   PLEASE ELABORATE ON THE NATURE OF COST SHIFT IN RATEMAKING.

 5   A.   To some extent cost shifts are an unavoidable consequence of the ratemaking process.

 6        Details and nuances of cost causation are inevitably blurred as a result of the aggregation,

 7        classification, grouping, and allocation that occurs with both costs and customers. The

 8        technical and interdependent nature of components in the electric system also complicates

 9        achieving a perfect allocation of costs in accordance with the principle of cost causation.

10               However, there are multiple types of cost shifts that we can generally describe. The

11        previous example of a cost shift or subsidization of rural customers by urban customers

12        could be considered an intraclass cost shift, or a cost shift that occurs between members of

13        the same customer class. Cost shifts can also occur between different customer classes as

14        an interclass cost shift, when, for example, residential customers are paying for costs

15        caused by industrial customers or vice-versa.

16               Other types of subsidization or cost shifts exist as well. There are intertemporal

17        (a.k.a. generational) cost shifts in which costs caused during one time period are paid by

18        customers in a different time period, either earlier or later. Another type of cost shift is an

19        interparty shift, where costs or risks that might otherwise be the burden of the utility or its

20        investors are shifted onto customers.

21   Q.   DO GEORGIA POWER CUSTOMERS EXPERIENCE COST SHIFTS?

22   A.   Cost shifts of various types exist throughout the Georgia Power system. Some, such as the

23        previously described intraclass cost shift between urban and rural customers, could be


                            Justin Barnes Direct Testimony, on behalf of GIPL
                                        GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                 Page 10

 1        considered structural since they result from the design of the basic ratemaking process.

 2        Other cost shifts, however, are the result of more deliberate choices.

 3                Consider, for example, some of the cost shifts associated with the Vogtle nuclear

 4        expansion project. Current customers are charged for Nuclear Construction Cost Recovery

 5        but may or may not receive future benefits from the construction for which they are paying.

 6        This is an example of an intertemporal cost shift where costs are charged to customers in

 7        one time period but benefits are received by customers in a different time period.

 8        Ratepayers in some future time will receive the benefits of electricity from this nuclear

 9        facility, but some of the ratepayers today who have been allocated these costs will never

10        receive the benefits of electricity from this facility.

11                The cost recovery for the Vogtle expansion project could also be considered an

12        interparty cost shift. Customer financing via construction work-in-progress (“CWIP”)

13        reduces the risk to other investors (e.g., equity and debt holders) and mitigates potential

14        risks to the Company if the facility does not operate as expected in the future. A full pass-

15        through of fuel costs presents a similar type of risk-shifting, as doing so places the entirety

16        of fuel price risk on customers rather than sharing that risk between customers and a

17        utility’s shareholders.

18   Q.   ARE YOU OBJECTING TO THE COST RECOVERY MECHANISMS USED FOR

19        VOGTLE COSTS OR FUEL COSTS?

20   A.   No, not in this testimony. I am simply pointing out that cost shifts: (a) exist in many forms,

21        (b) can be caused by the necessity of using approximations to define cost responsibility, as

22        well as intentional decisions, and (c) are inextricably linked to the perspective from which

23        one views the accuracy of the mechanisms used to define cost responsibility.

                                         GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                  Page 11

 1                   B.      Schedule RNR Monthly Netting and Schedule ECCR
 2
 3   Q.   ARE THERE OTHER EXAMPLES OF POTENTIAL COST SHIFTS IN GEORGIA

 4        POWER’S RATE PROPOSAL THAT WARRANT THE COMMISSION’S

 5        ATTENTION IN THIS PROCEEDING?

 6   A.   Yes. The Company alleges that the Schedule RNR monthly netting option creates a cost

 7        shift wherein monthly netting participants are being subsidized by non-participants. The

 8        Company has also proposed an adjustment to its proposed revenue requirement to recover

 9        a projected $1.4 million of revenue erosion which they have attributed to monthly netting

10        compared to compensation for exports to the grid at avoided cost. This purported cost shift

11        is the basis of the Company’s position that the Schedule RNR monthly netting option

12        should not be expanded to allow additional customers to enroll.

13                 The Company also proposes to continue the current design of Schedule ECCR,

14        which uses a percentage-based bill adder to charge customers for environmental

15        compliance costs, the bulk of which relate to costs incurred for remediation of CCR storage

16        sites.

17   Q.   HAS      THE    COMPANY          ADEQUATELY            DEMONSTRATED           THAT   THE

18        SCHEDULE RNR MONTHLY NETTING OPTION CAUSES A COST SHIFT TO

19        NON-PARTICIPANTS?

20   A.   Understanding that the Company has been directed to file supplemental testimony on this

21        issue, it did not do so in in its initial direct testimony for two reasons.

22                 First, revenue erosion should not be conflated with interclass or intraclass cost

23        shifting. Absent the Company’s proposed revenue adjustment, any revenue erosion would

24        be borne by the Company’s shareholders. Non-participant customers would be indifferent


                             Justin Barnes Direct Testimony, on behalf of GIPL
                                         GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                  Page 12

1         because their own rates would not be affected. In other words, the purported $1.4 million

2         cost shift to non-RNR ratepayers only exists because the Company created it by making

3         this revenue adjustment.

 4               Second, there are two facets to any question of cost shifting: (a) the costs to serve

 5        a group of customers, and (b) what they pay for service. The Company’s revenue erosion

 6        projection addresses only one side of this equation. A complete picture is only possible

 7        with a more extensive evaluation of the long-term costs that monthly netting participants

 8        impose on the system, including the costs that they avoid for all customers or cause to be

 9        avoided for by customers within their rate class.

10   Q.   IS THERE A REASON FOR THE COMMISSION TO GIVE CONSIDERATION

11        TO SHAREHOLDER INTERESTS IN REGARD TO THE PROJECTED

12        REVENUE EROSION?

13   A.   No. The purported revenue erosion is one very small piece of potential variations in utility

14        revenue, and the earnings band and sharing mechanism already adequately addresses the

15        interests of shareholders by allowing the Company to petition for incremental cost recovery

16        if its earned return on equity (“ROE”) falls below 9.5%. The Company does not propose

17        any changes to this mechanism in the current proceeding. This mechanism offers a global

18        solution to the potential for under- or over-earning with recognition that variations in

19        earnings are inevitable.

20               Carving out potential lost revenues from individual sources is counter to the

21        purpose of the earnings band framework, which does not entitle the Company to any

22        particular amount of revenue within the band. Stated another way, why should the

23        Company be permitted to recover additional revenue for the benefit of shareholders if it is


                            Justin Barnes Direct Testimony, on behalf of GIPL
                                        GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                 Page 13

 1        already earning an adequate return for those shareholders as defined by the lower boundary

 2        of the earnings band?

 3   Q.   PLEASE EXPLAIN WHY YOU ARE RAISING SCHEDULE ECCR DESIGN AS A

 4        MATTER FOR COMMISSION CONSIDERATION AS IT RELATES TO THE

 5        ISSUE OF COST SHIFTING.

 6   A.   The design of Schedule ECCR is a matter for close Commission attention because: (a) the

 7        amount of costs associated with CCR remediation is large (and will continue to grow), and

 8        (b) the present design is inconsistent with cost causation. Total proposed ECCR revenue is

 9        $937,513,791, or 10.6% of proposed overall total revenue. Schedule ECCR is not subjected

10        to a specific cost allocation protocol for the purpose of the distributing that revenue

11        requirement between customer classes. Rather, the allocation is effectively based on class

12        revenues because Schedule ECCR uses a standard percentage adder to customer bills. As

13        a consequence, Schedule ECCR effectively “enhances” every component of base rates,

14        such as fixed customer charges, demand charges, and the different varieties of energy

15        charges (e.g., on-peak, off-peak, individual tiers within Schedule R). This suggests that the

16        costs being recovered via Schedule ECCR are a mix of customer-related, demand-related,

17        and energy-related costs. However, this is not the case in practice. Rather, the bulk of costs

18        being recovered under Rider ECCR are for CCR remediation, which is energy-related in

19        character.

20   Q.   WHY SHOULD CCR REMEDIATION COSTS BE CONSIDERED ENERGY-

21        RELATED RATHER THAN DEMAND- OR CUSTOMER-RELATED?

22   A.   CCRs are produced when coal is burned as fuel. Every megawatt-hour (“MWh”) of

23        electricity generated from the combustion of coal generates a predictable quantity of CCRs.


                            Justin Barnes Direct Testimony, on behalf of GIPL
                                        GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                 Page 14

 1        Therefore, costs associated with CCRs are an energy-related cost and should be allocated

 2        on an energy basis. The creation of CCRs has no plausible connection to the number of

 3        customers on the system, nor does it have any relation to monthly demand peaks, maximum

 4        class demands, or levels of on-peak or off-peak energy use. The determinant of total CCR

 5        volume is total energy generated, therefore an energy allocator is appropriate.

 6   Q.   IS THERE ANY MERIT TO THE ARGUMENT THAT CCR IMPOUNDMENTS

 7        ARE FIXTURES TO COAL-FIRED GENERATION UNITS, AND THEREFORE

 8        SHOULD BE SUBJECT TO THE SAME ALLOCATION METHODOLOGY AS

 9        THE PLANT ITSELF?

10   A.   No. The impoundment could be considered a fixture, but the CCRs themselves are not

11        somehow tied to the plant. The very fact that in many cases CCRs must be relocated for

12        disposal, and the costs of that relocation are directly related to the volume that must be

13        moved, lends further support to their energy-related character. This is distinctly different

14        from capital investments in pollution control equipment that are made in order to continue

15        to allow a plant to operate to meet system demand and energy needs.

16   Q.   SHOULD THE FACT THAT SOME CCR REMEDIATION COSTS ARE

17        ASSOCIATED WITH RETIRED PLANTS AFFECT THE COST ALLOCATION

18        REGIME?

19   A.   No. Some amount of intergenerational cost shift will be present no matter how costs are

20        recovered from present customers. Newer customers will always shoulder a portion of the

21        burden of paying for the legacy costs of past users. There is no cost allocation regime that

22        is inherently fairer for addressing this intergenerational issue. However, an energy-based

23        allocation is fairer overall because: (a) a portion of the customer base did play a role in


                            Justin Barnes Direct Testimony, on behalf of GIPL
                                        GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                 Page 15

 1        causing those legacy costs due to their past energy use (i.e., there has not been 100%

 2        customer turnover), and (b) not all of the Company’s coal-fired generation units are retired

 3        so CCRs that require disposal are still being produced.

 4   Q.   HOW DOES THE CURRENT ALLOCATION OF CCR COSTS COMPARE TO AN

 5        ENERGY-BASED ALLOCATION?

 6   A.   The Company’s proposed rates allocate the residential rate group 50.6% of ECCR costs,

 7        of which the bulk are CCR remediation costs, resulting in a total allocation of roughly

 8        $474.1 million to residential customers. By contrast the residential customer class accounts

 9        for only 34.3% of total system energy requirements. If an energy allocator was used in

10        place of the present regime, residential customers would be allocated roughly $321.4

11        million, or approximately $152.7 million less than the Company’s proposal. The current

12        framework that causes residential customers to bear a disproportionate share of CCR

13        remediation costs is a clear cost shift in which residential customers are subsidizing

14        customer classes who cause greater costs by consuming of greater amounts of energy.

15   Q.   HAVE      REGULATORS          IN    OTHER       STATES       REACHED        THE     SAME

16        CONCLUSION THAT CCR REMEDIATION COSTS ARE ENERGY-RELATED

17        AND SHOULD THEREFORE BE ALLOCATED USING AN ENERGY FACTOR?

18   A.   Regulators in both Virginia and North Carolina determined that allocating costs associated

19        with CCR remediation on an energy basis was consistent with the principle of cost

20        causation. In Virginia, in a proceeding on the establishment of Dominion Energy Virginia’s

21        Rider CCR, the Hearing Examiner found “a direct connection between the volume of CCR

22        materials to be remediated … and the volume of fuel that was burned at the four Power


                            Justin Barnes Direct Testimony, on behalf of GIPL
                                        GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                 Page 16

 1           Stations over many years.” 4 Based on the established energy basis allocation of fuel-related

 2           costs and the consistency of applying “a uniform energy rate to recover all CCR

 3           remediation costs” with past fuel cost recovery “allocating … CCR costs on an energy

 4           basis is consistent with cost causation.” 5 Elaborating on this finding, the Hearing Examiner

 5           observed: (a) that although an energy-related allocation may result in higher costs to high-

6            load customers those high-load customers also experienced a greater share of energy-

7            related benefits from the combustion of coal, and (b) that allocating CCR costs on an energy

 8           basis was therefore “reasonable and equitable.” 6 The final order from the full Virginia State

 9           Corporation Commission agreed with and adopted this finding. 7

10                    In North Carolina, the North Carolina Utilities Commission (“NCUC”) likewise

11           concluded it was appropriate to “allocate all coal ash expenditures by the energy allocation

12           factor, rather than the demand-related production plant allocation factor.” 8 Duke Energy

13           Carolinas (“DEC”) had initially proposed to allocate coal ash costs on a demand basis, a

14           position opposed by several parties. After consideration, the NCUC ultimately agreed

15           “with Public Staff witness Maness that the amount of coal ash correlates with the amount

16           of energy produced from coal, and that the entire DEC system benefited from that energy.”

 6                                         A.       Flaws of Demand Rates

 7   Q.      PLEASE EXPLAIN IN GENERAL WHY DEMAND RATES ARE INCONSISTENT

 8           WITH THE PRINCIPLE OF COST CAUSATION.

 9   A.      Grid infrastructure costs are caused by aggregate customer contributions to peak demands

10           on different parts and levels of the system. A customer’s monthly non-coincident maximum

11           demand 16 only approximates their contribution to those costs for facilities in close

12           proximity to the customer, such as secondary service lines and line transformers. Even line

13           transformers will experience peaks that depart from individual customer peaks if they serve

14           multiple customers because the peak demands of individual customers often do not occur

15           at exactly the same time. The greater the number of customers (and different types of

16           customers) served by a given piece of infrastructure, the greater this diversity benefit

17           becomes.

18                    Non-coincident demand charges fail to account for this diversity and fail to account

19           for the time-differentiated nature of generation, transmission, and distribution capacity

20           costs. The departure from cost causation is particularly pronounced at the generation

21           capacity and transmission level where an enormous amount of load diversity is present, but


     16
        Non-coincident demand refers to a customer’s demand at any time rather than only during times that coincide
     with the collective peak demands on the system or a portion of the system.

                                  Justin Barnes Direct Testimony, on behalf of GIPL
                                              GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                       Page 23

 1              it also exists at a significant level on the distribution system as individual distribution

 2              circuits often serve thousands of customers with different electricity usage patterns.

 3   Q.         DO THE COST ALLOCATION METHODOLOGIES USED BY THE COMPANY

 4              REFLECT THIS DIVERSITY BENEFIT?

 5   A.         Yes. In the Company’s cost of service study, production demand costs are allocated based

 6              on class demands at the time of the 12 monthly peaks (“12CP”). Certain transmission costs

 7              are allocated based on only the monthly peaks during June – September (“Summer 4CP”)

 8              while the balance of transmission costs are also allocated according to the 12CP

 9              methodology. 17

10                       Distribution cost allocation uses a hybrid system under which a portion of

11              distribution costs are classified as customer-related according to the Company’s minimum-

12              intercept study and allocated based on the number of customers, and the remaining balance

13              of costs are classified as demand-related and allocated based on non-coincident maximum

14              class demand. This maximum class demand methodology assigns costs based on the

15              maximum demand of a given customer class during any single hour of the year. 18 Although

16              maximum class demand is sometimes referred to as a “non-coincident peak” allocator

17              because the timing of the maximum demand of a given class may not be coincident with

18              peak conditions on the broader system, this measure of demand still has a coincident

19              character since it measures customer demands coincident with the maximum demand of

20              the class as a whole. This is distinctly different from how a non-coincident demand charge

21              functions because a non-coincident demand charge is based on an individual customer’s


     17
          2022 Rate Case Hr’g Tr. Vol. 1 at 893-95 (Sept. 28, 2022).
     18
          Id. at 896-97.

                                     Justin Barnes Direct Testimony, on behalf of GIPL
                                                 GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                          Page 24

 1            demand at any time, regardless of whether that demand occurs during times when

 2            aggregate class demand or system demand are at their highest. 19

 3   Q.       DOES THE DEMAND CHARGE COMPONENT OF TOU-RD REFLECT THE

 4            TIME-DIFFERENTIATED CHARACTER OF DEMAND-RELATED COSTS?

 5   A.       No. The TOU-RD demand charge is based on a customer’s maximum demand during a 60-

 6            minute interval each monthly billing period regardless of when that demand occurs. That

 7            demand may be offset from the time periods that are likely to produce a peak on the system

 8            or within the residential customer class, and by using a single hourly value, the demand

 9            charge fails to reflect the frequency of customer demands on the system during potential

10            peak windows. Likewise, the demand charge does not reflect the summer-peaking

11            character of the Company’s system, which drives the Company’s generation planning and

12            is a component of the allocation methodology for transmission costs.

13   Q.       DOES THE TOU-RD RATE DESIGN PROVIDE A PRICE SIGNAL THAT

14            PROMOTES EFFICIENT USE OF ELECTRIC SERVICE?

15   A.       No. There are two problems with the design. First, demand charges in general provide an

16            inconsistent price signal to customers. Second, the price signal itself is not actionable for a

17            typical residential customer.

18   Q.       PLEASE EXPLAIN HOW THE TOU-RD PRICE SIGNAL IS INCONSISTENT.

19   A.       The inconsistency in the price signal arises from the fact that the marginal cost of demand

20            from a customer’s standpoint is highly diluted by previously registered maximum demands


     19
       The rationale for using maximum class demand for distribution cost allocation is that individual segments of the
     distribution system (e.g., a primary circuit) tend to primarily serve clusters of customers within the same rate class.
     In reality there can be considerable variations in the timing of peaks for individual substations or circuits in terms of
     both the time of year and the hour of the day.

                                    Justin Barnes Direct Testimony, on behalf of GIPL
                                                GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                         Page 25

 1           within a billing period. During a billing period, any demand below the amount of previous

 2           maximum demand has a zero marginal cost. Even if a customer’s maximum demand occurs

 3           during a peak window, they have no incentive to reduce their demands during future on-

 4           peak hours except as necessary to avoid exceeding a maximum demand amount registered

 5           earlier in the same billing period. Ultimately, this effect produces economically inefficient

 6           outcomes. For instance, during any given summer there are likely to be multiple heat waves

 7           with multi-day durations. An economically efficient rate design should incentivize a

 8           customer to reduce their demand as much as they can throughout the duration of peak

 9           conditions caused by these events. By contrast, demand rates progressively dilute the price

10           signal hour by hour and day by day as a billing period progresses, and fail to account for

11           the frequency and duration of high demands during peak periods.

12   Q.      DOESN’T THE VOLUMETRIC TIME OF USE COMPONENT OF SCHEDULE

13           TOU-RD PROVIDE THIS TYPE OF CONSISTENT PRICE SIGNAL?

14   A.      It does, but the price signal should be stronger. At the Company’s proposed rates, the fixed

15           and demand components of Schedule TOU-RD account for roughly 82% of total rate

16           revenue. The on-peak volumetric component accounts for only roughly 8.5% of total rate

17           revenue. 20 For comparison, the on-peak volumetric component of Schedule TOU-REO

18           accounts for approximately 20.2% of rate revenue 21 and the volumetric on-peak component

19           of Schedule TOU-PEV accounts for roughly 20.7% of total rate revenue. 22

 1   Q.   PLEASE EXPLAIN WHY THE TOU-RD RATE DESIGN DOES NOT PROVIDE

 2        AN ACTIONABLE PRICE SIGNAL TO CUSTOMERS.

 3   A.   The only way that a customer can reduce their costs under the TOU-RD rate design is to

 4        manage their electricity demand during every single hour of a monthly billing period, and

 5        ultimately do so consistently month after month. Such close attention to demand

 6        management is highly impractical for a typical residential customer, not to mention being

 7        unnecessary as a means of reducing system costs.

 8   Q.   CAN YOU ELABORATE ON WHY IT IS IMPRACTICAL FOR RESIDENTIAL

 9        CUSTOMERS TO EFFECTIVELY MANAGE THEIR DEMAND DURING ALL

10        HOURS?

11   A.   Yes. First, consider the summer months during which there are a total of 2,928 hours, each

12        of which may require the customer’s attention even if that hour falls outside of a peak

13        period. The notion that customers should just avoid using major appliances at the same

14        time is much harder to execute than it sounds, in particular because a single instance of

15        relative inattention (or personal need) can produce an outsized bill impact. For instance,

16        during the summer months when an air conditioner is likely to be cycling consistently, it

17        is next to impossible to avoid using an electric dryer during the same time period when the

18        air conditioner is operating. The same is true for other daily necessities, such as cooking

19        with an electric range or oven, not to mention other things like using a dishwasher, coffee

20        maker, toaster, or electric hair dryer. Furthermore, even relatively flexible needs are not

21        infinitely flexible due to family needs and schedules. These challenges are not limited to

22        the summer months. During the winter months any customer with electric heating is likely

23        to experience the same scheduling difficulties, incurring high bills and utility charges


                            Justin Barnes Direct Testimony, on behalf of GIPL
                                        GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                 Page 27

 1        despite the fact the Company does not identify a winter period during which it desires

 2        customers to manage their electricity usage.

 3   Q.   WHAT TYPES OF RATES PROVIDE A MORE CONSISTENT, ACTIONABLE

 4        PRICE SIGNAL THAN THE PRICE SIGNAL SENT BY DEMAND RATES,

 5        INCLUDING SCHEDULE TOU-RD?

 6   A.   Time-differentiated volumetric rates improve the price signal to make it more consistent

 7        by effectively charging customers for their average contribution to peak conditions. This

 8        provides the customer with the same price signal during all potential peak hours, such that

 9        electricity demand during each individual on-peak hour has a meaningful marginal cost.

10        This price signal should incent load shifting away from peak hours, not just those hours

11        where a customer might register a demand above a previous maximum demand. The typical

12        TOU price signal is also more actionable for customers because it presents a simple and

13        predictable risk-reward calculation that can be readily planned around and managed using

14        both technology adoption and behavioral changes.

15               On a practical level, consider again that the summer months during which there are

16        a total of 2,928 hours. The on-peak period applied for five hours on weekday non-holidays

17        would comprise only 14.5-14.9% of those hours depending on whether the holidays fall on

18        a weekday or a weekend. Clearly, managing energy use during on-peak periods is a more

19        manageable proposition than doing so during all hours. Moreover, managing an on-peak

20        TOU pricing period also allows the customer to focus their efforts on the highest value

21        hours from the standpoint of reducing stress on the system. This allows a customer to

22        employ technologies such as programmable and smart thermostats and other smart

23        appliances or devices (e.g., managed EV chargers) in support of their efforts, and adopt


                            Justin Barnes Direct Testimony, on behalf of GIPL
                                        GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                 Page 28

 1        consistent behavioral patterns for activities that are amenable to flexible timing (e.g., avoid

 2        using a dishwasher or an electric dryer).

 3   Q.   DO     SMART        APPLIANCES          REALISTICALLY            OFFER        CUSTOMERS

 4        OPPORTUNITIES FOR CUSTOMERS TO MANAGE DEMAND CHARGES?

 5   A.   No. Smart appliances are not an effective means to manage demand charges. Smart devices

 6        are suited towards management of predictable TOU pricing windows and response to

 7        demand reduction dispatch during critical peak periods, but they do not function as a means

 8        of reducing demand during all hours of a day as is required to manage a demand charge.

 9        For example, a smart thermostat or smart EV charger can be: (a) programmed to

10        concentrate operation during off-peak periods, and (b) respond to a demand reduction

11        dispatch signal during critical peak periods. However, neither of these capabilities are

12        sufficient to manage demand rate cost management because they depend on known,

13        targeted use management periods and targeted dispatch during unpredictable critical peak

14        periods. In fact, their use towards these ends would likely have the effect of concentrating

15        demand during other periods (e.g., overnight low-cost periods) resulting in a higher charge

16        to the customer, despite the fact that they are responding to a signal to reduce their

17        consumption during on-peak periods.

18               Demand rate management requires integrated, coordinated operation during all

19        hours among these end-uses, as all other electricity end-uses present in a residence. That is

20        not something that smart appliances themselves can manage. Such coordinated

21        management would require an entire “smart home” system where all end-uses are

22        controlled under an overarching objective of limiting demand at all times. Establishing an


                            Justin Barnes Direct Testimony, on behalf of GIPL
                                        GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                 Page 29

 1           integrated smart home is highly impractical for the vast majority of residential customers,

 2           whether they reside in new premises or existing homes.

 3   Q.      IS THIS VIEW OF RATE DESIGN AND ECONOMIC INEFFICIENCY SHARED

4            BY OTHERS?

5    A.      Yes. The Regulatory Assistance Project (“RAP”) recently published a Policy Brief (“RAP

 6           Policy Brief”), which I have attached to my testimony as Exhibit JRB-2. In examining the

 7           rationale for demand charges, RAP concludes that such charges have little or no place in

 8           modern rate design:

 9                       Demand charges as we’ve known them in the United States
10                       should largely become a relic of the past. Current forms of
11                       demand charges, based on 15-minute, 30-minute or 60-minute
12                       individual customer peaks and often intended to recover the
13                       lion’s share of capacity costs, are neither cost reflective nor
14                       efficient in general. For much of the 20th century, traditional
15                       demand charges may have been a second-best alternative that
16                       worked reasonably well for high-load-factor industrial
17                       customers. Developments of the past several decades have,
18                       however, made even this application of demand charges archaic.
19                       Such charges do not reflect the cost drivers of the modern
20                       electric system, and typical sizing of these charges are larger
21                       than justified by proper economic analysis of the electric system.
22                       Peak window demand charges, while an improvement over their
23                       traditional counterpart, do not solve many of the core
24                       deficiencies of demand charges as an efficient pricing
25                       mechanism. Time-varying rates, including TOU rates and
26                       critical peak pricing, are more efficient than peak window
27                       demand charges. 23

       MARK LEBEL & FREDERICK WESTON, REGULATORY ASSISTANCE PROJECT, DEMAND CHARGES: WHAT ARE THEY
     GOOD FOR? AN EXAMINATION OF COST CAUSATION at 7 (2020), https://www.raponline.org/wp-
     content/uploads/2020/11/rap-lebel-weston-sandoval-demand-charges-what-are-they-good-for-2020-november.pdf.

 1   Q.          WHY DO THE AUTHORS OF THE RAP POLICY BRIEF REACH THIS

 2               CONCLUSION?

 3   A.          They raise the issues that I have also raised, specifically that what matters for cost causation

 4               is not a customer’s individual peak, but their contribution to peak demands on the system

 5               (or a segment thereof), and that time-differentiated energy rates are more economically

 6               efficient than demand rates. They further observe that a significant portion of capacity

 7               investment is more properly classified as energy-related rather than exclusively demand-

 8               related because, “Put simply, not all capacity costs are incurred to meet peak demand. As

 9               a result, capacity costs for generation should either be split into the traditional demand-

10               related and energy-related categories, or else those categories should be updated into a

11               more modern time-based classification framework.” 24

1    Q.      ARE THERE ANY OTHER IOUS IN THE NATION THAT HAVE CLOSED

2            TRADITIONAL VOLUMETRIC RATE DESIGNS TO NEWLY CONSTRUCTED

3            RESIDENTIAL PREMISES?

4    A.      No. I am not aware of any other utility that has made a proposal of this type in recent years,

6            proposals to establish a demand rate component within the standard residential rate, but

7            none of those proposals have been adopted. There are no other IOUs in the country that

8            either: (a) use rates with demand charge components as default rates for new or existing

9            residential premises, or (b) otherwise apply them in a mandatory fashion in residential

10           rates. 25

11   Q.      WHAT WOULD BE A MORE ACCURATE CHARACTERIZATION OF TRENDS

12           IN RESIDENTIAL RATE MODERNIZATION?

13   A.      Generally, the trend is towards greater availability of different rate options for the

14           residential class, with an emphasis on making time-varying rates available as an additional

15           option to flat or tiered rates. To be sure, the availability of different rate options has often

16           included new optional demand rates, often with a time-varying element, in addition to

17           volumetric TOU rates. However, there is no trend towards migrating residential customers

18           to demand rates as GPC is seeking to do by using a demand rate as the default rate for new

19           premises and closing other volumetric rate options. Any assertion that such a trend exists

20           is simply inaccurate.

4            notified of their eligibility to do so, resulting in many remaining on a rate that was more

 5           expensive for them. 29 At the time it was estimated that roughly 5,000 of Delmarva Power’s

6            13,700 medium general service customers (36.5%) qualified for the non-demand small

 7           general service rate. 30

 8   Q.      HOW ARE THE EXAMPLES IN COLORADO AND DELAWARE RELEVANT

 9           TO RESIDENTIAL DEMAND RATES GIVEN THAT THEY ALL RELATE TO

10           NON-RESIDENTIAL RATES?

11   A.      The use of demand rates in rate designs for non-residential customers has historically been

12           common, in particular for larger customers, but the same is not true for residential rates.

13           This is in part because the prevalence of high load factor customers who benefit from

14           demand rate designs tends to increase with demand. In other words, many non-residential

15           customers subject to demand rates are accepting of them because the rate design costs them

16           less than a volumetric rate would. At the same time, demand rates applied to high load

17           factor customers may have a somewhat better alignment with cost causation because

18           relatively constant demands tend to make an approximation to a customer’s contribution

        Del. Pub. Serv. Comm’n, Docket No. 20-0217, Order No. 9564 at 5, April 1, 2020,
     https://delafile.delaware.gov/CaseManagement/ViewFileNetDocument.aspx?Id=5e265e84-c955-4ee9-a58d-
     319ea565a901&Type=Docket.

                                              GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                       Page 35

1         to peak demands based on a monthly maximum demand measurement somewhat more

2         accurate.

3                Residential customers in general are highly dissimilar to the types of high load

 4        factor customers for whom demand rates are beneficial and for whom cost causation may

 5        be fairly well-aligned (even if only incidentally). The Delaware and Colorado examples

 6        highlight the fact that, like most residential customers, not all small commercial customers

 7        fit this profile, and for those customers demand rates can be punitive and inconsistent with

 8        cost causation.

 9   Q.   CAN YOU PROVIDE ANY EXAMPLES OF REGULATORS REDUCING THE

10        ROLE THAT DEMAND RATES PLAY IN THE RESIDENTIAL RATE

11        CONTEXT?

12   A.   No, because demand rates are not currently deployed as default or standard residential rates

13        by any IOU in the country. As previously noted, none of the small number of utility

14        proposals in recent years to introduce demand charges into standard or default residential

15        rates have been adopted, so there is no role that demand rates play in residential rate design

16        that could be reduced or eliminated.

17   Q.   ARE THERE ANY OTHER INDICATIONS OF MOVEMENT TOWARDS

18        GREATER AVAILABILITY OF NON-DEMAND RATES TO DIFFERENT TYPES

19        OF CUSTOMERS?

20   A.   Yes. There is a prominent trend is taking place in the context of rates charged for non-

21        residential EV charging. Numerous utilities throughout the country now offer rates that

22        allow volumetric charges to be substituted for demand charges, or establish limits or caps

23        on demand charges for high capacity EV charging stations, in particular public direct


                            Justin Barnes Direct Testimony, on behalf of GIPL
                                        GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                 Page 36

 1           current fast charger (“DCFC”) stations. GPC is proposing one such rate in the current

 2           proceeding in the form of Schedule Charge It-Electric Vehicle (“CIEV”). Although this

 3           trend is associated with a specific challenge faced by high capacity EV charging, at its core

 4           it acknowledges the fact that demand charges can be punitive to customers with low load

 5           factors.

 6                         C.       The Schedule TOU-RD Default Rate Experience

 7   Q.      PLEASE DESCRIBE HOW SCHEDULE TOU-RD CAME TO BE DEPLOYED AS

 8           A DEFAULT RATE FOR NEW RESIDENTIAL PREMISES.

 9   A.      In the Company’s 2019 rate case, it proposed to make Schedule R unavailable to new

10           residential premises beginning in January 2020. The Settlement Agreement adopted in the

11           2019 rate case did not adopt this proposal, but did allow the Company to use Schedule

12           TOU-RD as the default rate for new residential premises starting in January 2021. This

13           means that new customers are placed on Schedule TOU-RD unless they opt into another

14           rate option when they begin service. The Settlement also obligated the Company to “report

15           back to the Commission at the time of its next base rate case regarding the adoption of

16           TOU-RD and its use as the default rate for newly constructed residential premises.” 31

 1   Q.   WHY WOULD THE SCHEDULE TOU-RD ENROLLEE USAGE PROFILE HAVE

 2        CHANGED SO SIGNIFICANTLY DURING 2020 AND 2021 RELATIVE TO

 3        PRIOR YEARS?

 4   A.   Customers with relatively higher average usage tend to be customers with high load factors,

 5        for whom demand rates are less costly than volumetric rates. High usage customers that

 6        benefited from being on the rate were the norm prior to 2020, as one would expect with an

 7        optional rate since participants self-select. Such a profound change in the customer

 8        composition strongly suggests that at best, customers were unaware that Schedule TOU-

 9        RD was not a good fit for their usage patterns, and at worst, they were steered towards

10        service under a rate that is not in their best interest from a cost standpoint.

11   Q.   IF THE TOU-RD IS MORE EXPENSIVE THAN ANOTHER AVAILABLE RATE

12        OPTION, WHY WOULD MOST CUSTOMERS REMAIN ON THE SCHEDULE

13        TOU-RD INSTEAD OF SWITCHING TO ANOTHER OPTION?

14   A.   Assuming that they even know they have the option to change to a different rate, there are

15        two possible reasons. First, Schedule TOU-RD has a one year minimum initial contract

16        term, which presumably prevents a customer from switching until they have received

17        service under Schedule TOU-RD for at least one year. It is not clear specifically how the

18        Company is enforcing this restriction for defaulted customers, but the letter of the tariff is

19        quite clear on this point, stating, “The Customer is required to remain on the TOU-RD


                             Justin Barnes Direct Testimony, on behalf of GIPL
                                         GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                  Page 46

 1            tariff for a period of twelve (12) months from the contract date. … The customer may

 2            change tariffs at any time after the initial twelve (12) month term expires.” 42

 3                     A second reason could be that they simply do not know any better. Recall that the

 4            customers being defaulted are residing in newly constructed premises. Customers may be

 5            moving from outside the Company’s service territory and be wholly unfamiliar with the

 6            Company’s rates, or from within the service territory from a dissimilar prior residence (e.g.,

 7            apartment to single-family home, a different apartment building, or a single-family home

 8            with different electric end-uses and/or square footage). Those customers do not have the

 9            benefit of being able to compare bills under Schedule TOU-RD to a bill under a different

10            rate because they lack a suitable point of comparison.

11   Q.       ARE THERE ANY OTHER NOTABLE PATTERNS PRESENT IN YOUR

12            EVALUATION OF HOW TOU-RD HAS AFFECTED PARTICIPANTS DURING

13            RECENT YEARS?

14   A.       Yes. The excessive costs are concentrated during the non-summer off-peak months, in

15            particular the “shoulder” spring and fall seasons. This is illustrated in Figures 3 and 4,

16            which show that the difference between the effective volumetric rates that Schedule TOU-

17            RD customers pay compared to what customers would pay with the other rate options is at

18            its highest during the shoulder months. These shoulder months are characterized by lower

19            overall demands on GPC’s system, meaning that demand during these periods is not a

20            driver of system costs. The fact that the effective rates for Schedule TOU-RD customers

 5   Q.        IS THERE ANY JUSTIFICATION FOR THESE HIGH NON-SUMMER RATES

 6             BEING PAID BY SCHEDULE TOU-RD CUSTOMERS, SUCH AS ADDRESSING

 7             WINTER PEAKS?

 8   A.        No, for several reasons. First, the highest effective rates appear during the shoulder months,

 9             not the winter months. Second, the Company has expressly stated that it does not believe

10             there is a need for a winter peak period in its residential TOU rates at present. 43 Third, such

11             a justification would conflict with the design of Schedule R and the Company’s two other

12             available TOU rates, which offer lower rates during non-summer months. It is

13             unreasonable for such a material difference in price signal to exist between available

14             residential rates, and Schedule TOU-RD is the outlier in this respect. The problem is not

15             the design of other available residential rates. The problem is the design of Schedule TOU-

16             RD.
