to shift load from inside to outside that window.49 Nevertheless, peak window demand
charges share many of the faults of traditional monthly demand charges, just on a
different scale. Once again, the key distinction is between the consistent and symmetric
marginal incentive of a time-varying kWh rate and the arbitrary effects driven by the
demand charge’s ratchet.

A close examination of customer behavior reveals why energy-based prices are preferable
to demand charges even within a peak window. In any system with significant customer
diversity, a large number of customers will not have their individual peaks at the time of
the system’s peak. Still, it could be that a substantial number of customers peak at the time
of the system peak. The proportion of one to the other matters if demand charges are to
have a significant linkage to the system peak. Customers who are at risk of setting the
individual peak for the demand charge face a high marginal price for consumption, but
those who are not face a lower marginal price. This proportion will vary from service
territory to service territory and over time as technology evolves.

Customer behavior under a peak window demand charge would likely even vary based on
completely arbitrary factors. That could be whether certain customers are at the beginning
of their billing period or whether a significant event that led a customer to incur a largely
unavoidable peak (e.g., hosting a party during a peak window) happened before that very
high-load time. This randomness can be entirely avoided. The fair and efficient solution is
to continue to treat all consumption as marginal, a condition that is achieved by time-
varying kWh rates.

In the absence of technology that automates response to changes in prices, the ratchet
problem for peak window demand charges may be diminished by the inability of
customers to respond accurately to its incentive structure. It is unlikely that people going
about their daily lives can do more than respond to the broad incentives provided by either
an on-peak kWh price in a simple TOU rate or a peak-window demand charge. In both
cases, the easiest answer may very well be just “consume less during the peak window
period.”50 This could mitigate the harm posed by the ratchet, but it also begs the question
about the underlying rationale if there is no customer response.

A modest subset of residential customers may be able to respond to the next rule of thumb
presented by a peak window demand charge: to operate as few end uses as possible
simultaneously. Fully responding to the incentives posed by a demand charge requires

However, energy management technology, enabled by software and “supercharged” by

responses to demand charges do not typically optimize use of the system.

Peak window demand charges also create intraclass cost allocation problems, which are
linked closely to the above efficiency concerns. Peak window demand charges still
overcharge the low-load-factor customer and undercharge the high-load-factor customer.

Even well-designed TOU rates do not necessarily reflect critical peak times very well. For
example, a four-hour weekday on-peak window for only the highest demand months will
include around 200-400 hours annually. These will necessarily contain some days with
higher peaks than others and only a limited number of hours that define utility capacity
needs for reliability purposes at peak. Simple TOU rates do not distinguish in this regard
between the moderate peaks (e.g., ordinary days in the summer) and the very highest
peaks (e.g., extremely hot days in the summer). In short, the implication is that simple
TOU rates do not provide a sharp enough incentive on actual peak days.51 In any case, we
are no longer bound to simple TOU pricing. Dynamic rates, including critical peak pricing,
peak-time rebates, variable peak pricing and real-time pricing, all better address peaking
issues because they provide higher marginal prices at the times of maximum system stress.
By concentrating customer attention on the hours that actually drive costs, the more
dynamic rates produce better results for the electric system and society.

By its very nature, a demand charge cannot present symmetric and consistent marginal
incentives in the same way as a time-varying kWh charge. Compared to traditional
demand charges, properly sized peak window demand charges have a better cost causation

retain demand charges at all?

4. What Might Be Left for Demand
Charges?
The foregoing demonstrates that the typical argument for demand charges, as used for
generation, transmission and shared distribution capacity, is substantially flawed. Even so,
we want to investigate if there are any circumstances, however limited, for which demand
charges are an efficient rate design.

Some theorists have identified a different and, in our minds, much narrower set of
rationales for demand charges. The case for time-varying rates relies substantially on the
diversity of load and the lack of a direct relationship between individual customer peaks
and the system peaks that drive costs. A diverse set of customers may, in the aggregate,
create a predictable load profile much of the time. But what if this diversity goes away in
an unpredictable manner? Or, for that matter, in a predictable one? Is there something
about the causation of costs in special and limited circumstances that warrants charging
for peak incurrences of short-term (e.g., 15-minute) demand for individual customers?
To answer this question, we consider three cases that, on their faces, might present a
marginal-cost justification for demand charges. The first is one that we have carved out
from the beginning: capacity costs that are not shared, such as dedicated transformers and
service drops, which we term “dedicated site infrastructure.”53 This illustrates some
important issues relevant to any broader theoretical case for demand charges. The second
is the cost associated with uncertainty in customer behavior. The third is timer peaks, a
phenomenon where customers shift usage in response to hours with lower prices.

52
     RAP authors, writing with partners from Synapse Energy Economics, previously recommended daily-as-used demand charges for standby
service to large combined heat and power customers, as an alternative to monthly standby demand charges. The purpose was to recognize
that different combined heat and power customers would have scheduled and forced outages on different days and could share the same
capacity to provide their standby service. This was certainly an improvement on monthly demand charges for such customers, but, in light of
the progress made in metering and time-varying energy-based rate structures, there’s every reason to think today that such time-varying

4.1 Dedicated Site Infrastructure
Dedicated transformers and service drops for individual customers are, by definition, not
shared infrastructure. The relative importance of this category of cost will vary by
customer class. Larger commercial and industrial customer classes, as long as they are
taking secondary voltage service, will often have dedicated transformers for each customer
or a dedicated transformer bank for customers taking three-phase power. Dedicated
transformers will be rare for residential customers in urban and suburban areas, but
single-family homes will almost always have a dedicated service drop. The largest
industrial customers may have their own primary line (effectively serving as a dedicated
service drop) or a dedicated substation (effectively serving as a dedicated transformer).
In rural areas, each customer will typically have a dedicated transformer, at which point
transformers are customer-specific site infrastructure.

For these customer-specific site infrastructure costs, there is no diversity of demand
between the customer meter and point of connection with the shared system. As a result,
individual customer NCPs are certainly relevant to the sizing of these components. One
might conclude from this that a demand charge can provide a reasonable pricing incentive
here. The time period for such a demand charge should have nothing to do with a shared
peak since there is no sharing of the infrastructure. Nor should it be limited to peak
windows since the peak for an individual customer could occur at any time. The cost of
these components may be no more than about $1/kW/month, a fraction of typical demand
charges.54

There are also other ways of efficiently pricing this category of costs. A similar set of
customer incentives may be presented by a connected load charge for a set amount of local
capacity. Such a connected load charge can help with efficient sizing, but only if it’s
accompanied by a fee for overages or the automatic tripping of circuits when demand
would cause an overage. Even then, a connected load charge provides no incentive for
customers to manage their usage efficiently; that is, there are no cost savings to be gained
by keeping their demand below the level of the predetermined connected load. A charge
that establishes the relationship of the customer’s individual peak demand to the sizing of
these components might, however, give the customer some incentive to minimize peaks.

It is worth examining this issue at the level of engineering and planning. What type of
customer behavior would minimize the risk of transformer overload and degradation?
Or what type of customer behavior would allow utilities to size dedicated transformers
more efficiently?

Capacity ratings for the different elements of the electric system are set with many

necessarily incurring significant damage. As Tom Short colorfully puts it, a conductor
rated 480 amps “will not burst into flames at 481 [amps].”55

This type of short-run marginal cost pricing does not resemble a demand charge and has
the virtue of linking closely in time the incurrence of high marginal costs to the prices
charged. These approaches are quite sophisticated and could be costly to administer. To
achieve a rate that is more feasible now, a simpler structure would be necessary. A daily-
as-used demand charge or a traditional monthly demand charge, based on 15-minute
or 30-minute peaks, could certainly discourage the extremely high short-term peaks that
would damage a transformer. Those options might not do enough, however, to discourage
a sustained, multihour overload.

4.2 Risks of Customer Variance at Peak Times
Load diversity isn’t static and can fluctuate in ways that are both predictable and
unpredictable. Predictable changes often occur around the weather, one of the few
variables that simultaneously affects all customers in a given area. Regarding
unpredictable changes, consider a simple hypothetical illustrated in Figure 8.

If there are 10 “random-load”                              Figure 8. Two hypothetical load patterns randomly chosen

The risk of a peak of 88 kW or higher drops from 10.9% to 3.1%, and the risk of a peak of

type of risk goes down as the number of customers increases.59 However, if the customer
choices are correlated, between hour 2 and hour 3 in this hypothetical, the risk does not
necessarily decrease with a higher number of customers.

REGULATORY ASSISTANCE PROJECT (RAP)®                                              DEMAND CHARGES: WHAT ARE THEY GOOD FOR? |                     35


This simple example is the essence of the argument made by Michael Veall.60 He
demonstrates that, for a given level of average customer demand during a peak, higher
variance customers lead to a risk of higher peaks, particularly if they are correlated. This,
in turn, results in a need for higher capacity planning margins. Veall constructs a detailed
economic model of optimal peak period pricing. He states that the traditional monthly
demand charge does not reasonably address this issue, but rather a peak window demand
charge can serve as marginal price on a customer’s variance. He notes additional caveats:
“If there are many small users with uncorrelated demands, the effects of an individual
user’s variation on total system variation will be small. But if users are large or their
demands are correlated, variance charges are important.”61 Finally, Veall’s result
demonstrates that, if a peak window demand charge is to be imposed, it should be paired
with an on-peak kWh rate.62 The logic around risk and Veall’s theoretical model present an
argument for a peak window demand charge that is substantially different from those that
utilities put forward. And again, we see a more defensible justification for peak window
demand charges for larger-volume customers. But the key question of correlations and
levels of risk has been neglected in the discussion around demand charges and is only a
theoretical possibility in Veall’s model. Furthermore, Veall’s model does not consider the
possibility of more granularly dynamic time-varying kWh rates.

Marcel Boiteux, the influential French economist and executive for Électricité de France
(EdF), does discuss risk and uncertainty in a 1952 paper, written jointly with his colleague
Paul Stasi.63 When it comes time for tariff design, Boiteux and Stasi describe two different
zones of the shared electric system: (1) the “collective network” and (2) the “semi-
individual network, whose capacity depends particularly on the uncertainties of
consumption of each customer.”64 With respect to the collective network, they find that the
“uncertainties of individual consumption” are small enough to be ignored.65 And, finally,
their analysis of the “semi-individual network” is dominated by risk and the irregularities
of individual customer’s loads. This leads them to a justification for a complex system of
subscription-based contract demand charges, with higher prices for contracted demand in

generalities as to the demarcation of the semi-individual network:

              The extent of the zone within which the uncertainties of individual
              demands have a very marked influence on the collective cost is greater in
              proportion to the irregularity of the demands considered, and to the
              correlations among these demands. This extent depends also on the density
              of consumption, for the number of customers supplied from a given node
              plays an important role in the “reduction of uncertainties.”66


Based on these considerations, Boiteux and Stasi largely describe the generation and
transmission system (150-220 kV) as the “collective network” and the distribution system
(15-60 kV) as the “semi-individual” network.67 They are discussing these issues in the
context of the then-new Tarif Vert for high voltage industrial customers, and the
discussion could be read in a manner that is limited to those customers. This could mean
that the dividing line for the semi-individual network could vary by the size of customer.
Whether residential customer fluctuations are correlated in a significant and pertinent
way is another empirical question Boiteux and Stasi do not address. It is unclear whether
the irregularities of individual residential customers would ever be significant enough to
matter at a level higher than a shared transformer.

4.3 Timer Peaks
Michael A. Crew and Paul R. Kleindorfer (1979) raise another area where a demand charge
could theoretically be efficient, which they describe as the secondary preferences of
customers, given the structure of time-varying rates, and the shifting of demand to
notionally off-peak times. This is colloquially known as a timer peak. This occurs if
customers increase their usage substantially during hours with low rates or more
specifically right at the time when low-priced hours begin.68 In the worst-case scenario,
TOU rates can theoretically just shift the system peak without reducing it if enough usage
is shifted to hours with low prices. The same is true of coincident peak window demand
charges. This outcome can be avoided by managing the number of periods in the rate, the
hours covered by each period and the relative prices. One utility has designed a TOU rate
in which each customer chooses a three-hour peak period of 4-7 p.m., 5-8 p.m. or 6-9 p.m.
All of these customers have 6-7 p.m. in their peak period; two-thirds of them have 5-6 p.m.
and 7-8 p.m. in their peak period; and one-third have either 4-5 p.m. or 8-9 p.m. in their

66
     Boiteux & Stasi, 1964, p. 123
67
     Boiteux & Stasi, 1964, p. 110.
68
     Bonbright mentions this as a possible objection to time-of-use rates. See Bonbright, 1961, p. 362, fn 23: “In Chapter 10 of his book already
cited in footnote 10, Davidson suggests this type of rate [time of day and time of season] as preferable to the familiar Hopkinson-type rate. But
among the objections to it is the danger that its sharp breaks will create surges in the loads imposed on a power station or on a distribution

peak period. This provides the utilities with the most powerful pricing signal during the
most likely peak hour but substantial peak reduction in the adjacent hours.69 Another
simple solution is to apply different hours to different classes or subclasses. For example,
single-family residences may have their tariff shifted one hour earlier than apartments, or
secondary general service one hour later than primary general service.

If the more general system peaks are not impacted significantly enough by this
phenomenon to warrant changing the structure of the rate, more granular and local issues
can theoretically arise. Figure 9 shows a set of results from a San Diego Gas and Electric
rate for electric vehicles, where the “super off-peak” rate begins at midnight.70


Figure 9. Real-world illustration of timer peak with EV charging on TOU rate


                      Source: Jones, B., Vermeer, G., Voellmann, K., & Allen, P. (2017). Accelerating the Electric Vehicle Market


This is a rational customer response to a TOU rate, at least for specific end uses. If an
electric vehicle is parked at home in the evening and will not be used again until morning,
then the customer has a significant amount of flexibility to choose when charging will
begin. The very beginning of the lowest price period is an obvious time to start charging.
While this may not present an issue at the generation and transmission level, assuming
midnight remains an off-peak period, bunching of EV charging could lead to issues at the
more local level.

Again, thinking about a line transformer helps focus the analysis. If five single-family
homes are served by one shared transformer and all five of those homes have EVs that
start charging at midnight, then impacts at the line transformer level are a possibility.
Furthermore, what if those houses have other timed usage that starts at the beginning of
the lowest price period? Sending a secondary price signal that discourages households


69

https://www.mjbradley.com/sites/default/files/MJBA_Accelerating_the_Electric_Vehicle_Market_FINAL.pdf

from turning on all of their major end uses at midnight could be effective. A daily-as-used
demand charge can send such a signal if it were applied across 24-hour periods. A more
traditional monthly demand charge, however, will send that signal in a much more
attenuated way. A connected load charge based on a contract demand for the cost of
connection, with fees for overages, similar to the Électricité de France Tempo rate for
residential customers,71 would send a similar price signal as well.

There are other ways to deal with this phenomenon besides price signals with demand-
charge features. The beginning of the off-peak period with the lowest price could be
staggered for different customers, for example, beginning at 10 p.m. for one-third of
customers, midnight for another third and 2 a.m. for the last third. For customers with
long-duration controlled loads, like water heaters or electric vehicles, this would be easy
for the customer to manage and beneficial to the utility. To maximize the benefits of such
an approach, one would need to have a relatively even split among those three options for
the customers on each shared transformer. Load management programs and smart
devices could deal with this type of issue as well. For some loads, particularly water
heating and EV charging, we anticipate advanced devices that will enable the utility to
manage loads to minimize costs and enable customers to benefit from even lower off-peak
rates for enabled devices.

One could even question how much of a problem this poses to the longevity of the shared
transformers in question. The ambient temperature has almost always cooled off by
midnight, and several hours of low or moderate loads could allow the transformer to cool
from significant levels of usage during the day or early evening. In certain circumstances,
it could be more convenient and cost-effective to upgrade any potentially affected
transformers, particularly where multiple water heaters or EV chargers are served from a
single transformer.


5. Conclusion
Demand charges, of either the traditional monthly NCP or peak window variety, are not
efficient, as a general matter, for shared system capacity costs because:

•       For the vast majority of customers, any peak reduction signal in a traditional monthly
        demand charge is weak and inaccurate.

•       Traditional calculations for demand charges have included far too many costs as
        demand-related. Ideally, utility commissions will adopt a new time-based classification


71
     Electricite de France. (n.d.). Tarif Bleu: Regulated sale tariff for electricity. https://particulier.edf.fr/en/home/energy-and-
services/electricity/tarif-bleu.html


                                               Justin Barnes Direct Testimony, on behalf of GIPL
                                                           GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                         Exhibit JRB-2 | Page 39 of 42

REGULATORY ASSISTANCE PROJECT (RAP)®                                              DEMAND CHARGES: WHAT ARE THEY GOOD FOR? |   39


        and allocation framework for generation, transmission and shared distribution costs.72
        Failing that, the numerous energy benefits from capacity investments should be
        properly accounted for — that is, reflected in energy, not demand, charges.

•       Simple TOU rates are superior to peak window demand charges in their own right, but
        AMI enables time-varying energy charges, such as critical peak pricing, peak-time
        rebates and variable peak pricing, that much more accurately target times of system
        stress and reward end users for shifting their loads to off-peak times.

Although we have shown the significant downsides to using current forms of demand
charges, in very limited circumstances there might be cost- and efficiency-related
justifications for certain types of demand charges. But such charges would be significantly
lower than those prevailing for industrial customers in the United States today. Dedicated
site infrastructure is a small portion of utility system costs, and typical demand charges
would not necessarily provide an optimal signal to control these costs. The primary
concerns around timer peaks are almost certainly limited to local infrastructure.

As for the general risk of customer variance and correlation, little work has been done to
investigate the statistical bases of this more sophisticated case for demand charges. We
think that it is unlikely that such an analysis would find that a substantial demand charge
would be fairer or more efficient than time-varying energy charges. Lastly, there is a better
case for demand charge-like structures for large customers, who are more likely to have
significant dedicated site infrastructure. One might also argue that high variance at peak
times among these customers has a more significant chance of influencing the overall
system peak. Any such demand charges may not look like Hopkinson rates and would
likely be only a second-best solution to a sophisticated system of time-varying energy
charges.

The economic and regulatory principles that underlie these judgments are not new. The
inescapable essentials of microeconomic theory are at work here. Boiteux, Bonbright and
Kahn follow these principles and theories, as do the other scholars and practitioners we
cite. In 1964, Paul Garfield and Wallace Lovejoy73 also stepped into the fray. They
converted principles of economic efficiency and fairness into straightforward criteria for
assessing the merits of cost allocation methods and rate designs for generation and
delivery capacity costs:

•       All utility customers should contribute to capacity costs.

•       The longer the period of time that customers preempt others’ use of capacity, the more
        they should pay for the use of that capacity.


72
     Lazar et al., 2020.
73
     Criteria adapted from Garfield, P., & Lovejoy, W. (1964). Public utility economics, pp. 163-165. Prentice Hall.


                                             Justin Barnes Direct Testimony, on behalf of GIPL
                                                         GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                       Exhibit JRB-2 | Page 40 of 42

40   |   DEMAND CHARGES: WHAT ARE THEY GOOD FOR?                         REGULATORY ASSISTANCE PROJECT (RAP)®


•    Any service that makes exclusive use of a portion of capacity should be assigned all of
     the costs for that portion of capacity.

•    The allocation of capacity costs should change gradually with changes in the pattern of
     usage.

•    More capacity costs should be allocated to on-peak usage than off-peak.

•    Interruptible service (or other forms of utility restrictions and control) should be
     allocated less in capacity costs as the degree of restriction increases.

Only time-varying energy charges can meet all of these objectives simultaneously. Demand
charges for shared costs are demonstrably less efficient and less equitable than they.

 5   Q. THERE               IS     A     SIGNIFICANT                 DIFFERENCE              BETWEEN   YOUR
 6        RECOMMENDATIONS AND GEORGIA POWER’S RECOMMENDED ROE AND
 7        EQUITY RATIO. HOW DO YOU EXPLAIN THAT?
 8   A. The divergence arises from differences in both the models and input assumptions used to
 9        determine our respective ROE and equity recommendations.
10            Georgia Power’s cost of capital expert, Mr. James Coyne, uses four models in developing
11        his recommended return on equity (ROE). Two of those models, the Risk Premium Analysis
12        (RPA) and Expected Earnings Analysis (EEA), both suffer from a severe, invalidating
13        conceptual flaw: they are based on utilities’ authorized or forecast return on equity, not their
14        actual cost of equity (COE), or the “the return to the equity owner … commensurate with
15        returns on investments in other enterprises having corresponding risks.” 2 Thus, these two
16        models are not commonly used in finance outside of utility regulatory proceedings because
17        they do not actually estimate the cost of equity. These models are akin to developing a nutrition
18        recommendation based on what people actually eat, not on what they should eat to maintain a
19        healthy weight.
20            The other two models used by Mr. Coyne – the discounted cash flow model (DCF) and
21        capital asset pricing model (CAPM) – are widely used throughout finance to estimate the cost
22        of capital. But Mr. Coyne’s implementations of each suffer from numerous flaws which bias
23        his results upward.
24            In implementing the DCF, Mr. Coyne uses unnecessarily long trailing price histories to
25        calculate the dividend yield, which bias his figures upward, and he assumes demonstrably
26        unrealistic, economically impossible long-term dividend growth rates.
27            In implementing the CAPM, he uses an interest rate forecast long and widely known to be
28        systematically upwardly biased. He cherry-picks a beta calculation methodology that does not
29        reflect current investor risk perceptions and applies the “Blume” adjustment that is not valid

 1       for utilities, both of which upwardly bias his results. He fails to examine other, more robust
 2       beta estimation methodologies, investigate whether the pandemic-related changes in market
 3       conditions and investor perceptions of utility risk were temporary or have been sustained, or
 4       compare his results to the long-term history of utility betas.
 5           Mr. Coyne’s chosen methodology does not reflect the wide range of ways beta could be
 6       estimated, each of which could produce dramatically different results. As Nobel laureate
 7       Fischer Black, one of the pioneers of empirical testing of beta and the CAPM, famously
 8       admonished, “Watch out for data mining!” 3 – running an analysis several different ways but

 1              C.      Organization of testimony

 2   Q. HOW IS YOUR TESTIMONY ORGANIZED?
 3   A. First, I review a few key conceptual issues related to the cost of capital and capital structure.
 4         Next, I provide a detailed assessment of Mr. Coyne’s cost of equity estimation methodology
 5         and implementation. For the DCF and CAPM, the two of Mr. Coyne’s four cost of equity
 6         models that are valid, I explain various modifications to his methodology and assumptions to
 7         correct for the deficiencies in Mr. Coyne’s analyses and then provide the resulting COE
 8         estimates. I then apply the capital structure concepts reviewed in the first part of my testimony
 9         to determine the optimal equity ratio that minimizes customer costs while satisfying the
10         demands of equity and debt investors. Finally, I estimate the potential savings to customers
11         from adopting my recommended ROE and equity ratio instead of Mr. Coyne’s proposal.
12   II.        CONFUSION BETWEEN THE RATE OF RETURN ON CAPITAL AND COST OF
13              CAPITAL HAS LED TO EXCESSIVE AUTHORIZED RETURNS.

14              A.      Rate of return on capital and cost of capital are not the same: rate of return
15                      on capital is a financial performance metric, whereas cost of capital is the
16                      measure of economic cost described in the Hope case.

17   Q. WHAT IS THE OBJECTIVE IN SETTING A UTILITY’S AUTHORIZED RATE OF
18         RETURN?
19   A. The authorized rate of return is the amount of money, expressed as a percentage of capital
20         invested, that a utility is allowed to recover in customer rates to compensate debt and equity
21         investors for assuming the risks of investing in the utility
22              The Supreme Court provides the guiding ratemaking principles in its 1944 Hope Natural
23         Gas case, in which it directs ratemakers to arrive at “just and reasonable rates” by a “balancing
24         of the investor and the consumer interests.” 6 Consumer interests are straightforward: they want
25         to minimize costs and rates. Investors include holders of both the utility’s debt and equity. A
26         utility’s debt investors expect to receive their contractual interest payments. Debtholders
27         therefore have a “legitimate concern with the financial integrity of the company whose rates
28         are being regulated,” 7 i.e., the utility’s credit quality and anticipated ability to fulfill its


     6
         320 U.S. 591, 603.
     7
         Id.


                                      Justin Barnes Direct Testimony, on behalf of GIPL
                                                  GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                           Page 7

                                      PUBLIC DISCLSOURE VERSION


1              obligations to debtholders. Equity investors expect a fair return, defined in Hope as
 2             “commensurate with returns on investments in other enterprises having corresponding risks.” 8
 3   Q. HOW DOES THE RATE OF RETURN ON CAPITAL DIFFER FROM THE COST OF
 4             CAPITAL?
5    A. The rate of return on capital, often shortened to “rate of return,” is an accounting metric of
 6             financial performance, calculated by dividing the value returned to investors – e.g., interest,
 7             net income – by the amount of capital invested. The cost of capital is the return investors expect
 8             on their investment. It is referred to as a “cost” because it reflects what investors demand in
 9             return for assuming the risk of the investment and, therefore, what companies must pay for that
10             investment. The rate of return on each form of capital, whether calculated retrospectively or
11             estimated prospectively, may or may not equal its respective cost of capital.
12   Q. HOW DOES THE AUTHORIZED RATE OF RETURN ON CAPITAL DIFFER FROM
13             THE RATE OF RETURN AND THE COST OF CAPITAL?
14   A. The authorized rate of return refers to a specific use of this accounting metric to determine a
15             utility’s revenue requirement and customer rates. According to long-established ratemaking
16             principles, which will be explained in more detail below, the authorized rate of return should
17             be set equal to the cost of capital. Figure 2 summarizes the differences between these three sets
18             of metrics for debt, equity, and the combined return.

2    Q. WHAT PRINCIPLES DO YOU USE TO DETERMINE YOUR RECOMMENDED
3          AUTHORIZED RATE OF RETURN?
4    A. As the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners (NARUC) has explained,
5          “Fundamental financial concepts demonstrate that the fair rate of return to use in ratemaking
6          for a utility is its cost of capital in order to achieve the proper balance between customers and
 7         investors.” 9 Mr. Coyne has also acknowledged, in ROE testimony in other jurisdictions, “that
 8         the allowed rate of return should equal the cost of capital.” 10 The objective in setting a utility’s
 9         authorized rate of return should, therefore, be to set the rate of return on each source of capital
10         – debt and equity – as close as possible to the actual cost of each source of capital.
11   Q. DOES THE APPROACH TO CALCULATING COST OF EQUITY DIFFER FROM
12         THE APPROACH TO CALCULATING COST OF DEBT?
13   A. Yes. The cost of outstanding debt can be directly determined from its contractual interest rates.
14         Similarly, the cost of debt expected to be issued can be accurately determined from known
15         interest rate indexes for debt of comparable credit quality, such as Moody’s utility bond

 1         indexes, which, in turn, are based on interest rates directly observed in the market. In contrast,
 2         the cost of equity, both existing and to-be-issued, cannot be directly observed and must be
 3         estimated using various models.
 4   Q. WHY IS THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN THE COST OF CAPITAL AND RATE OF
 5         RETURN IMPORTANT?
 6   A. The cost of capital and rate of return (on capital) are entirely different concepts. The rate of
 7         return is a financial performance metric. The cost of capital is an economic concept.
 8         Nonetheless, they are frequently referred to interchangeably in utility regulatory proceedings,
 9         perhaps in part because finance professionals commonly refer to the cost of capital as the
10         expected return (on capital). 11
11             The muddling of the difference between the cost of capital and the rate of return is not just
12         of semantic concern, particularly for the cost of equity, which must be estimated using various
13         models rather than directly observed (like the cost of debt).
14             This confusion between the cost of capital and the return on capital has infiltrated some of
15         the models commonly used in utility cost of capital proceedings to estimate the cost of equity.
16         These models’ apparent influence on regulatory decisions, though, does not make them correct
17         or mean they provide a suitable basis for estimating the cost of equity.
18             Models that rely exclusively on historical or forecast utility rates of return on equity,
19         without reference to utilities’ actual cost of equity, should be rejected outright. Mr. Coyne uses
20         two such models, one relying exclusively on historical authorized ROEs, the other on forecast
21         ROEs. These models incorporate no information about the actual cost of equity and are
22         therefore inherently flawed and produce invalid results. Consistent with the fairness principle
23         described by NARUC, and Mr. Coyne’s own statements, only models that estimate the cost of
24         equity should be used to determine the authorized ROE.


      11
           See, e.g., TIM KOLLER, MARC GOEDHART ET AL., VALUATION, 5TH ED. MCKINSEY & CO. 35 (2010): “The cost of
           capital is the price charged by investors for bearing the risk that the company’s future cash flows may differ
           from what they anticipate when they make the investment. The cost of capital to a company equals the
           minimum return that investors expect to earn from investing in the company. That is why the terms expected
           return to investors and cost of capital are essentially the same. The cost of capital is also called the discount
           rate, because you discount future cash flows at this rate when calculating the present value of an investment, to
           reflect what you will have to pay investors” (emphasis in original).

 1            B.      Multiple, diverse sources of evidence demonstrate that utilities’ authorized
 2                    ROEs far exceed their cost of equity.

 3   Q. DO AUTHORIZED ROES REFLECT THE ACTUAL COST OF EQUITY?
 4   A. No. Substantial, robust evidence suggests that authorized ROEs for nearly all U.S. utilities
 5         exceed their cost of equity. Georgia Power’s ROE follows this national pattern. Below, I
 6         provide three diverse analyses that compellingly demonstrate, individually and collectively,
 7         the substantial gap between authorized ROEs and utilities’ actual cost of equity: expected
 8         equity return forecasts produced by investment professionals, utility market-to-book ratios, and
 9         the increasing spread between authorized ROEs and interest rates.

10                    1.      Investment firms’ expected return forecasts for the U.S. equity market
11                            as a whole – which is riskier, on average, than utilities – are consistently
12                            lower than utilities’ authorized ROEs.

13   Q. ARE THERE OTHER PUBLIC SOURCES FOR COST OF EQUITY ESTIMATES
14         OUTSIDE UTILITY REGULATORY PROCEEDINGS?
15   A. Utility cost of capital proceedings are not the only purpose for which expected returns on equity
16         are estimated. Investment firms, such as JP Morgan, BlackRock, and T. Rowe Price, regularly
17         publish capital market assumption reports (CMAs) – expected return forecasts for various asset
18         classes. Figure 3 summarizes a survey of U.S. equity market return forecasts published by over
19         thirty firms in 2021.
20            The CMA forecasts shown in Figure 3 are grouped by assumed investment horizon: less
21         than ten years, ten years (the most common), and more than ten years. 12 The average across
22         the longer-term 10-year and more-than-ten-year horizons, 5.7%, is approximately 40% less
23         than the average ROE authorized for regulated utilities throughout the United States in 2021,
24         9.5%. 13 Not a single one of the forty-two expected return forecasts that I reviewed 14 is as high
25         as the average ROE yielded by any of Mr. Coyne’s models.

 1                      2.       Market-to-book ratios reveal that utilities’ cost of equity is
 2                               substantially lower than authorized ROEs.

 3   Q. WHAT IS A MARKET-TO-BOOK RATIO?
 4   A. “Market” value refers to the price one must pay to purchase a share of a company’s stock at
 5         any given time. “Book” value refers to the net equity invested in a company. In general, market
 6         value reflects the discounted value of a company’s future cash flows, while book value reflects
 7         the historical investment in the company. The market-to-book ratio (M/B) is a commonly used
 8         financial metric that indicates the amount of shareholder value added in excess of shareholders’
 9         return expectations.
10   Q. HOW DOES A MARKET-TO-BOOK RATIO RELATE TO RETURNS?
11   A. It is a well understood financial principle that a market-to-book ratio greater than 1.0 indicates
12         the company is expected to earn a return on its investment in excess of the actual cost of capital.
13         A positive net present value (NPV), i.e., the value of a company minus its investments, is the
14         signature indicator of a rate of return that exceeds the cost of capital. NPV is equal to
15         investment multiplied by (M/B – 1.0), so M/B exceeding 1.0 indicates that NPV is positive.
16   Q. WHAT DO UTILITY STOCK MARKET-TO-BOOK RATIOS REVEAL ABOUT
17         ROES RELATIVE TO UTILITIES’ COST OF EQUITY?
18   A. It has long been recognized that utilities’ market-to-book (M/B) ratios provide insight into the
19         relationship between authorized return and the true cost of capital. Legendary regulatory
20         economist Alfred Kahn 16 called attention to this phenomenon over fifty years ago in his 1970
21         classic, The Economics of Regulation: Principles and Institutions:

22                           [T]he sharp appreciation in the prices of public utility stocks, to
23                           one and half and then two times their book value during this
24                           period, reflected … a growing recognition that the companies in
25                           question were in fact being permitted to earn considerably more
26                           than their cost of capital. … The source of the discrepancy
27                           between market and book value has been that commissions have
28                           been allowing r’s [returns on equity] in excess of k [market cost
29                           of equity]; if instead they had set r equal to k, or proceeded at

           airline-deregulation-dies-93.

 1   Q. IN PRACTICAL, DOLLARS-AND-CENTS TERMS, WHAT DOES IT MEAN FOR A
 2         UTILITY TO HAVE A MARKET VALUE THAT IS HIGHER THAN ITS BOOK
 3         VALUE?
 4   A. In practical terms, this means that, for every dollar of equity a utility invests, shareholders
 5         receive back not just their investment plus a reasonable return, which would be the case when
 6         M/B = 1.0, but additional value equivalent to their equity investment multiplied by (M/B –
 7         1.0). At current M/B ratios near 2.0, authorized ROEs effectively double the value of utilities’
 8         equity investments, on top of returning their cost of equity. Such high returns are not necessary
 9         to attract capital and needlessly increase customer costs.
10   Q. ARE YOU ABLE TO CALCULATE GEORGIA POWER’S MARKET-TO-BOOK
11         RATIO?
12   A. Georgia Power is not publicly traded, so its market value is not directly observable.
13         Nonetheless, The Southern Company’s market-to-book ratio, averaging 2.82 over the month
14         of September 2022, 22 provides a reasonable estimate.

 1                      3.      Authorized ROEs and interest rates have diverged without a
 2                              corresponding increase in utilities’ risk profile.

 3   Q. WHY DO REGULATORS APPROVE AUTHORIZED ROES IN EXCESS OF
 4         UTILITIES’ ACTUAL COST OF EQUITY?
 5   A. A mathematical model called the Pólya urn can provide insight into why regulators have
 6         continued to approve authorized ROEs in excess of utilities’ actual cost of capital. 34 Historical
 7         return on equity decisions can be thought of as balls in an urn. To decide on a new case, the
 8         regulator draws a ball from the urn. The ball is then replaced, along with a new ball –
 9         representing the current ROE decision – with the same value. This process of sampling-with-
10         replacement-plus-duplication has a self-reinforcing property sometimes called the rich-get-
11         richer or Matthew effect.
12             Of course, this model is over-simplified because regulators look at other information
13         besides past authorized ROEs. The basic model can be modified to include additional balls in
14         the urn representing new information, such as the estimated current cost of equity. Nonetheless,
15         as long as regulators look at, much less rely on, past ROEs, changes in authorized ROEs will
16         lag changes in the current true cost of equity.
17             The basic utility regulatory model and risk profile have not changed significantly for
18         decades, so the utility equity risk premium – the spread of the cost of capital over risk-free
19         government interest rates – has remained stable. The Pólya urn model predicts that, in a market
20         in which interest rates and, assuming a relatively stable utility equity risk premium, utilities’
21         cost of equity have been trending downward for decades, authorized ROEs will consistently
22         exceed the actual cost of equity, and the spread will widen over time.
23             The data confirm the Pólya urn model’s prediction of such a widening spread between
24         authorized ROEs and the actual cost of equity. Figure 6 shows the quarterly average authorized
25         ROE for all U.S. utilities, the 30-year Treasury rate, and their difference. While interest rates
26         have declined steadily since the mid-1980s, authorized ROEs have not kept pace. As a result,
27         the ROE-Treasury spread has more than tripled, from approximately 2.3% in the early 1980s
28         to 7.1% in the two years through September 2022. It can be estimated from the Pólya urn model

4        setting ROEs higher and higher relative to utilities’ actual cost of equity unnecessarily raises
5        rates and costs to customers.

2    III.       ROE AND CAPITAL STRUCTURE ARE INTERRELATED AND CANNOT BE
3               DETERMINED SEPARATELY.

 4              A.       ROE and capital structure are interrelated through ROE’s impact on cash
 5                       flow.

 6   Q. DOES THE CAPITAL STRUCTURE IMPACT CUSTOMER COSTS?
 7   A. Yes. Capital structure refers to the share of a utility’s investment that is funded by debt and
 8          equity. Because equity generally has a higher cost than debt, assuming no change in authorized
 9          ROE, a higher equity ratio tends to increase customer costs.
10   Q. DOES THE CAPITAL STRUCTURE IMPACT A UTILITY’S CREDIT QUALITY?
11   A. Yes. A primary determinant of a company’s credit quality – its anticipated ability to repay its
12          debts – is the amount of debt outstanding relative to the total amount of capital, both debt and
13          equity, invested in the company. In general, a higher equity ratio tends to improve a utility’s
14          credit quality. Equity ratio is not the only determinant of credit quality, though. As will be
15          explained in more detail below, credit quality is also determined by the amount of cash
16          available to service the debt.

 6   Q. HOW SHOULD A UTILITY’S CAPITAL STRUCTURE BE DETERMINED?
 7   A. The appropriate capital structure can be determined more rigorously by using the analytical
 8         methods and metrics employed by credit rating agencies and as described by Mr. Fetter. The
 9         level of debt that can be accommodated in the capital structure will vary with ROE, because
10         funds from operation (FFO), a key determinant of a utility’s creditworthiness, is based on net
11         income, and net income is based on ROE, for any given credit rating and its corresponding
12         FFO/debt ratio.
13             Figure 8 illustrates the relationships between equity ratio, ROE, and FFO/debt. The
14         horizontal axis is the equity ratio; the vertical axis is FFO/debt. The light orange horizontal
15         band represents the range of FFO/debt that corresponds to the utility’s desired credit rating.
16         The dark orange arcing lines correspond to different levels of authorized ROE, with increasing
17         line thickness representing increasing ROE. Holding the equity ratio constant, FFO/debt
18         declines as the ROE is reduced (moving down from a thicker ROE line to a thinner line). But
19         the decline in FFO/debt when ROE is reduced can be reversed by increasing the equity ratio
20         (moving along the thinner ROE line up and to the right). Any number of combinations of ROE
21         and equity ratio can meet the level of FFO/debt needed to maintain the utility’s credit rating.
22         A higher ROE requires less equity to maintain the same FFO/debt and credit rating; a lower
23         ROE can maintain the same FFO/debt and credit rating if it is paired with a higher equity ratio.

 1   IV.       MR. COYNE EMPLOYS FLAWED MODELS AND ASSUMPTIONS THAT
 2             SYSTEMATICALLY PRODUCE UPWARDLY BIASED ROE ESTIMATES FOR
 3             GEORGIA POWER.

 4             A.      Mr. Coyne’s methodology relies, in part, on conceptually flawed models.

 5   Q. HOW DOES MR. COYNE ESTIMATE GEORGIA POWER’S ROE?
 6   A. Mr. Coyne employs four different models to estimate Georgia Power’s ROE: (1) constant-
 7         growth discounted cash flow model (CG DCF); (2) capital asset pricing model (CAPM); (3)
 8         risk premium analysis (RPA); and (4) expected earnings analysis (EEA). In the CG DCF,
 9         CAPM, and EEA, Mr. Coyne estimates ROEs for a number of proxy group companies and
10         bases his recommended ROEs on the proxy group average.
11   Q. WHAT IS YOUR OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF MR. COYNE’S APPROACH?
12   A. Although two of Mr. Coyne’s models, the CG DCF and CAPM, are widely used by financial
13         professionals and utility cost of capital experts to estimate the cost of equity, his
14         implementations are deeply flawed. They rely on unrealistic, systematically upwardly biased
15         assumptions that invalidate their results. I describe these deficiencies in more detail in Sections
16         IV.C and IV.E below.
17             The other two models, RPA and EEA, while frequently used by utility cost of capital
18         experts, are not commonly used elsewhere in finance outside utility regulatory proceedings,
19         and both suffer a severe, invalidating conceptual flaw.
20   Q. WHAT IS THE INVALIDATING CONCEPTUAL FLAW IN THE RPA AND EEA?
21   A. Both the RPA and EEA confuse the cost of equity and the return on equity, estimating the cost
22         of equity from historic or forecast returns on equity. The RPA consists of a linear regression
23         model of historical quarterly-average authorized ROEs against historical quarterly-average 30-
24         year Treasury yield. Mr. Coyne’s EEA estimates the cost of equity using ROE forecasts
25         provided by investment research firm Value Line. The primary drivers of Value Line’s ROE
26         forecasts for the proxy group companies, in turn, are the companies’ most recent authorized
27         ROEs. 48
28             Both the RPA and EEA are essentially models of past ROE decisions, not the actual cost
29         of equity. By design, therefore, they repeat the historic overearnings arising from the excess

 1        ROEs authorized in the past. As explained in Section II.A above, the cost of equity and the

 3        or should be equal. In fact, as explained in Section II.B above, authorized ROEs have diverged
 4        dramatically from utilities’ actual cost of equity, as reflected in the disparity between
 5        authorized ROEs and substantially lower forecast returns for the U.S. equity market as a whole,
 6        despite the latter’s higher risk; utility market-to-book ratios exceeding 1.0 for decades; and the
 7        growing divergence between average authorized ROEs and interest rates. Basing a utility’s
 8        authorized ROE on historically authorized ROEs without any reference to the actual cost of
 9        equity, as both the RPA and EEA do, merely perpetuates these errors.
10           A simple calculation illustrates the EEA’s conceptual flaw in equating ROE and COE.
11        ROE is the ratio of earnings to the book value of equity. But investors cannot buy shares at
12        book value; they must pay market value. The market value of the stocks Mr. Coyne chose to
13        include in his peer group tend to trade at a significant premium over book value, currently an
14        average of 2.1x. Mathematically, if investors pay more than book value for the same stream of
15        earnings, their expected return, i.e., the cost of equity, must be less than the ROE calculated
16        using the book value. 49 For companies earning just their cost of equity, the expected return,
17        i.e., the cost of equity, can be estimated by dividing earnings per share (EPS) by equity book
18        value per share (BVPS). 50 EPS can be expressed as the product of ROE and book value per

14            B.      Mr. Coyne fails to account for differences in equity ratios among the proxy
15                    group members.

16   Q. HOW DOES THE EQUITY RATIO AFFECT THE COST OF EQUITY?
17   A. All else equal, a lower equity ratio tends to raise the cost of equity. This can be understood
18         intuitively. The cash generated by a business is pledged to holders of its debt and equity, with
19         debtholders having first priority. As the equity ratio declines, a smaller share of the cash goes
20         to equity owners. To the extent there is uncertainty in the cash generated, it is amplified by a
21         lower equity ratio, increasing the riskiness of those cash flows. This increased risk is reflected
22         in a higher cost of equity.
23            The companies in Mr. Coyne’s proxy group have different equity ratios, and their average,
24         53%, 59 is different from the 56% he proposes for Georgia Power, so their costs of equity cannot
25         be used to estimate Georgia Power’s under his proposed equity ratio. In addition, Mr. Coyne
26         compares the equity ratios on a book basis; this is incorrect. When determining the cost of
27         capital, the market value of equity should be used. 60

 4          C.      Mr. Coyne’s DCF model uses upwardly biased dividend yield calculations and
 5                  unrealistically extrapolates analyst earnings growth forecasts into perpetuity,

 7   Q. WHAT IS YOUR ASSESSMENT OF MR. COYNE’S DCF MODEL?
 8   A. Mr. Coyne uses the constant-growth version of the DCF model (CG DCF) in his analysis, with
 9      a growth rate equal to equity analysts’ consensus 3-to-5-year EPS growth rate estimates. The
10      key shortcoming in his implementation of the CG DCF is the assumption that dividends can
11      grow at analysts’ estimated EPS growth rates into perpetuity. This economically impossible
12      assumption upwardly biases his results dramatically.
13   Q. PLEASE DESCRIBE THE CONSTANT-GROWTH DCF MODEL.
14   A. The constant-growth DCF is based on the well-known and widely used mathematical formula
15      for the value of a growing perpetuity stream of cash flows. It assumes a single, constant rate
16      of cash flow growth. In the constant-growth DCF model used by Mr. Coyne and many other
17      modelers, the cash flows are expected dividends, and the perpetuity value formula can be
18      expressed as:
                                                                (1 + 𝑔𝑔)

                                                                (𝑘𝑘 − 𝑔𝑔)
20      where 𝑀𝑀0 refers to the current market value (stock price), 𝐷𝐷0 , the current dividend (typically
21      four times the most recent quarterly payment), 𝑔𝑔, the forecast perpetuity growth rate, and 𝑘𝑘,
22      the cost of equity. Rearranging terms, the cost of equity can be expressed as a function of the

                                                     𝑔𝑔

 1        annual, payment of dividends. Mr. Coyne uses this approach. 61 Typically, the cost of equity is
 2        estimated for each member of the proxy group, with the mean or median reflecting the cost of
 3        equity for the target company. Mr. Coyne uses the mean.
 4            The general DCF model, which can allow for varying growth rates over time, is a
 5        particularly apt representation of stock returns because its assumptions realistically reflect
 6        several key features of share prices and expected returns. First, the DCF model’s perpetual
 7        cash flow stream assumption mirrors equity’s claim on a firm’s cash flows into perpetuity.
 8        Second, the assumption of steady growth in dividends over time reasonably reflects their much
 9        greater stability relative to other potential measures of profitability, like earnings or cash flow.
10        Third, the resulting single discount rate into perpetuity is consistent with the no-arbitrage
11        principle of finance. If investors expected higher (lower) returns in the future, they would
12        impute that into the price today and bid up (down) the price accordingly, such that near-term
13        and long-term returns roughly equilibrate. 62
14            But the constant growth version of the DCF used by Mr. Coyne is not well-suited for
15        estimating the cost of equity for a utility or any other stock, for two reasons. First, it is not
16        realistic to assume that a utility will maintain its current 3-to-5-year growth rate into perpetuity.
17        At any given time, the 3-to-5-year growth rate will deviate from its long-term trend due to any
18        number of factors, such as weather; economic conditions; new capital projects; regulatory, tax,
19        and other policy changes; and unforeseen events like the Covid-19 pandemic. Second, the
20        results of the CG DCF are particularly sensitive to the perpetuity growth rate assumption. The
21        inaccuracy introduced by assuming a relatively short-term growth rate will be sustained forever
22        invalidates the results of Mr. Coyne’s CG DCF. Mr. Coyne’s use of analyst estimates, a source

        most recent quarterly dividend is already slightly conservative relative to a more accurate quarterly model, and
        this adjustment is therefore not necessary.

 1         widely known to be upwardly biased, for his growth rate assumption further invalidates his

 3                    1.      Mr. Coyne’s dividend yield calculations use unnecessarily long trailing
 4                            price histories, introducing upward bias to his estimates.

 5   Q. HOW DOES MR. COYNE CALCULATE THE CURRENT DIVIDEND YIELD?
 6   A. To calculate the dividend yield, Mr. Coyne divides four times the most recent quarterly
 7         dividend by the trailing average share price over 30, 90, and 180 trading days. 63
 8             While it is advisable to use a multi-day average of the share price to reduce the effect of
 9         any day-to-day price fluctuations that are not reflective of investors’ long-term expectations,
10         all three of Mr. Coyne’s averages are unnecessarily long. Because share prices have a general
11         tendency to trend upward over time, the longer the backward-looking averaging period, the
12         lower the share price will tend to be, introducing upward bias into the dividend yield.
13         Averaging the most recent month of data, approximately 21 trading days, better balances the
14         competing objectives of mitigating the potential short-term volatility cited by Mr. Coyne and
15         reflecting current investor expectations.

16                    2.      Mr. Coyne’s perpetuity growth rate is based on analysts’ 3-to-5-year
17                            growth rate forecasts, producing economically impossible results.

18   Q. HOW DOES MR. COYNE ESTIMATE EACH PEER UTILITY’S PERPETUITY
19         GROWTH RATE?
20   A. While estimating the current dividend yield is fairly straightforward (although, as just
21         explained, the potential for bias exists even there), estimating the perpetuity growth rate is
22         more subjective. Mr. Coyne uses analysts’ consensus 3-to-5-year estimated earnings-per-share
23         (EPS) growth rate provided by Value Line, Thomson First Call (as reported by Yahoo!
24         Finance), 64 and Zacks. 65

 1            The DCF is a model of dividends, not earnings, so it would be preferable to use explicit
 2         dividend-per-share (DPS) forecasts. While some analysts, such as Value Line, provide DPS

 4   Q. IS IT REASONABLE TO ASSUME ANALYSTS’ CONSENSUS GROWTH RATES
 5         INTO PERPETUITY IN A DCF MODEL?
 6   A. No. There are several problems with using analysts’ estimates for the perpetuity growth rate.
 7         A wealth of academic research over decades has found that analyst forecasts tend to be
 8         optimistic. 66 Several other observations and analyses demonstrate the unreasonableness of
 9         using analysts’ 3-to-5-year EPS growth rate estimates for the perpetuity dividend growth rate
10         in the constant-growth DCF model.
11   Q. WHAT IS YOUR FIRST OBSERVATION OR ANALYSIS THAT DEMONSTRATES

13         RATE ESTIMATES FOR THE PERPETUITY DIVIDEND GROWTH RATE IN THE
14         CG DCF?

16         one decade, much less into perpetuity. Figure 10 compares the forecast aggregate earnings of
17         the U.S. publicly-traded companies for which analysts provide EPS growth forecasts 67 to
18         forecast U.S. GDP. 68 Currently, these companies’ combined earnings are equal to roughly 8%
19         of U.S. GDP. Yet if analysts’ growth projections were correct, they would exceed total U.S.

 2   Q. GIVEN THE NUMEROUS SHORTCOMINGS OF ANALYSTS’ FORECASTS,
 3         SHOULD THEY BE USED AT ALL IN DCF MODELS?
 4   A. Discounted cash flow models can be a robust approach to estimating expected returns and are
 5         widely used throughout finance. The key shortcoming of the constant-growth version of the
 6         DCF model – assuming a relatively short-term growth rate into perpetuity – can be easily
 7         remedied by assuming that analysts’ estimated growth rates apply only for a limited period,
 8         after which they converge toward a market- or sector-average terminal growth rate in a multi-
 9         stage DCF model (MS DCF), which I describe in more detail in IV.D below. Despite the
10         various deficiencies in analysts’ estimates even in the short-term, they are viewed as the best
11         available estimates of near-term investor expectations. That said, relatively little weight should
12         be placed on them in estimating the cost of equity, and the MS DCF model can weight them
13         more appropriately.

 1                 3.      Mr. Coyne’s flawed DCF results should be disregarded.

 2   Q. WHAT IS YOUR CONCLUSION REGARDING MR. COYNE’S DCF RESULTS?
 3   A. Mr. Coyne’s DCF model results should be disregarded completely. While, in principle, a
 4      constant-growth DCF model could be used to estimate the cost of equity, Mr. Coyne’s
 5      implementation is deeply flawed. Its dividend yield calculations use excessively long historical
 6      price data series, introducing upward bias into the results. More critically, Mr. Coyne’s DCF
 7      unrealistically assumes analysts’ EPS growth estimates are valid for forecasting dividends into
 8      perpetuity. Several analyses demonstrate the invalidity of this assumption: the economic
 9      impossibility of sustaining EPS growth forecasts even for one decade, much less into
10      perpetuity; the low correlation between analysts’ EPS and DPS growth forecasts; the unknown
11      starting period for analyst growth forecasts and therefore likely inconsistency with the DCF
12      model’s starting period; the inconsistency between the CG DCF results and analysts’ own
13      implied expected return estimates; and the wide disparity between analyst forecasts and
14      utilities’ long-term historical DPS growth rates.

15         D.      The Multi-Stage DCF should be used instead of the CG DCF because it allows
16                 more realistic cash flow projections, yielding more accurate results.

17                 1.      The multi-stage DCF model enhances the CG DCF by allowing
18                         different dividend growth rates over time.

19   Q. WHAT IS THE MULTI-STAGE DCF MODEL?
20   A. The multi-stage DCF model (MS DCF) enhances the CG DCF by allowing different dividend
21      growth rates over time. As we saw previously, analysts’ estimated 3-to-5-year growth rates are
22      too high to be sustained in perpetuity, and may be biased. But analyst estimates should not be
23      ignored completely. Analysts’ estimated 3-to-5 year growth rates provide useful information
24      about the relative expected growth across companies. Over the long term though, it is
25      reasonable to assume investors expect growth rates, in real terms, to revert to their long-term
26      historical trends. The MS DCF explicitly models different growth rates over time.
27         The MS DCF can incorporate any number of stages. For equity valuation, a three-stage
28      model is commonly used, in which the initial stage uses analysts’ estimates over their 3-to-5-
29      year forecast horizon, and the terminal stage uses the long-term real historical growth rate plus
30      current long-term inflation expectations. In between lies a transition phase, typically 5 to 15

 7         precedent exists for the MS DCF model, in both its two- and three-stage forms, in both
 8         corporate finance and regulatory contexts. 87
 9              In my implementation of the MS DCF, I assume an initial growth stage of three years – the
10         low end of analysts’ EPS growth rate forecast horizon, to mitigate the effect of their upward
11         bias – and a 10-year transition. To account for the quarterly distribution of dividends, I convert
12         the reported rates to quarterly and multiply the number of periods in the initial and transition
13         phases by 4. 88 The dividend yield is the most recent quarterly dividend divided by the average
14         price over December 2021.

 1   Q. HOW DO YOU ESTIMATE EXPECTED LONG-TERM INFLATION?
 2   A. For expected long-term inflation, I use Treasury-TIPS spreads. TIPS are Treasury Inflation-
 3         Protected Securities, which provide investors a return equivalent to inflation plus the quoted
 4         TIPS yield. The difference in yield between Treasurys and TIPS of equal maturity is a current
 5         measure of the market’s forward-looking inflation expectation over the life of the bonds.
 6             The MS DCF uses inflation for the terminal, not initial or transition, growth rate, so
 7         inflation into perpetuity is estimated at the end of the transition phase, not from today. I use

 9         the difference in the 30-year and 20-year Treasury-TIPS spreads:

 2   Q. DO YOU USE THE MS DCF ELSEWHERE IN YOUR ANALYSIS?
 3   A. Yes. I use it as one of two methods to estimate the market risk premium for the CAPM.

 4             E.        Mr. Coyne makes unrealistic, upwardly biased assumptions for all three
 5                       inputs into his CAPM.

 6   Q. WHAT IS THE CAPITAL ASSET PRICING MODEL?
 7   A. Mr. Coyne’s analysis incorporates another well-known COE model, the capital asset pricing
 8         model (CAPM). It estimates the cost of equity, 𝑘𝑘, from the formula:
 9                                                    𝑘𝑘 = 𝑟𝑟𝑓𝑓 + 𝛽𝛽�𝑟𝑟𝑚𝑚 − 𝑟𝑟𝑓𝑓 �
10         where 𝑟𝑟𝑓𝑓 is the risk-free rate (typically a long-term U.S. Treasury), 𝑟𝑟𝑚𝑚 is the expected return
11         on the market, and 𝛽𝛽 is a measure of risk of the company in question relative to the market.
12         The market risk premium (MRP), the difference between the market return and the risk-free
13         rate, 𝑟𝑟𝑚𝑚 − 𝑟𝑟𝑓𝑓 , reflects the additional return investors require as compensation for taking on
14         equity market risk. The CAPM is a simple model of the fundamental financial risk-reward
15         trade-off: investors demand higher returns as risk increases.

 1                  1.     The source of Mr. Coyne’s risk-free rate assumption has a long and

3    Q. WHAT RISK-FREE RATE DOES MR. COYNE USE IN HIS CAPM?
4    A. Mr. Coyne uses the 30-year Treasury (T30). Because the models estimate the expected return
5       on equity, which is a claim on cash flows into perpetuity, the longest-term rate available should
6       be used. The 30-year Treasury is the longest-term risk-free rate, so the T30 is an appropriate
7       term. Mr. Coyne calculates his CAPM COE estimates using both recent historical average and
8       forecast Treasury rates.
 9   Q. DO YOU HAVE ANY CONCERNS WITH MR. COYNE’S RISK-FREE RATE
10      ESTIMATES?
11   A. Yes, I have two concerns. First, as with the average price calculation for the dividend yield in
12      his DCF model, Mr. Coyne’s historical T30 averaging period, 30 days, is too long. Curiously,
13      Mr. Coyne provides no explanation for the use of different averaging periods in the two
14      different models. One month of trading data, typically 20-22 days, is sufficient. Nonetheless,
15      the difference in trailing averaging periods for interest rates generally does not introduce any
16      bias in the results because, unlike stock prices, which tend to exhibit an upward trend over
17      time, daily movements interest rates are random.
18   Q. WHAT IS YOUR SECOND CONCERN WITH MR. COYNE’S RISK-FREE RATE
19      ESTIMATES?
20   A. My second concern involves his use of a forecast rate. Using a forecast rate creates
21      inconsistencies with the time horizon of the DCF, which is estimated as of today (or, more
22      precisely, as of the end of the trailing price averaging period). The mathematical formula for
23      the present value of a periodic time series upon which the DCF is based discounts the stream
24      of future cash flows to a “time zero” one period before the first payment. The resulting discount
25      rate is as of that time zero. The first payment in the DCF model is typically assumed to occur
26      one time step from today; therefore, the rate determined by the DCF model is as of today.
27      Using an interest rate expected at some future date in the CAPM produces a COE as of that
28      future date, not today, and that COE is not directly comparable to the DCF’s COE.
29          Ignoring the consistency concern, even if we did want to use a forecast rate, in general,
30      commonly available interest rate forecasts are no better predictors of future interest rates than
31      the current market rate. Most importantly, though, I am particularly concerned about Mr.

 3             The predictive validity of current rates has been acknowledged among utility cost of capital
 4         experts. Reviewing the academic research, Roger Morin, author of the frequently cited
 5         practitioner text, New Regulatory Finance, concludes, “The literature suggests that on balance,
 6         the bond market is very efficient in that it is difficult to consistently forecast interest rates with

17   Q. HOW DOES MR. COYNE ESTIMATE THE BETA IN HIS CAPM MODEL?
18   A. Mr. Coyne uses beta estimates from two different financial data providers, Value Line and
19         Bloomberg. He uses Value Line’s betas as reported. Mr. Coyne overrides Bloomberg’s default
20         settings and uses only a subset of the beta estimates Bloomberg provides, such that the
21         calculation methodology and resulting beta estimates he reports for Bloomberg are very similar
22         to Value Line’s.
23             Importantly, Mr. Coyne selects two nearly identical beta calculation methodologies among
24         the multitude of methodologies commonly used by practitioners and academics, specifically
25         the two that currently tend to produce the highest results.
26   Q. HOW DO BLOOMBERG AND VALUE LINE ESTIMATE THEIR BETAS?
27   A. Both Bloomberg and Value Line estimate beta from the slope of a linear regression model of
28         a stock’s returns against the returns of the market overall. Both calculate “raw” betas from a

1    Q. WHY DO BLOOMBERG AND OTHER FINANCIAL DATA PROVIDERS USE
2       DIFFERENT BETA CALCULATION METHODOLOGIES, PROVIDE MULTIPLE
3       ESTIMATES, AND ALLOW USERS TO OVERRIDE THEIR DEFAULTS?
4    A. Beta is intended to be a forward-looking measure of relative risk, so it is inherently uncertain.
5       It cannot be measured directly (like an interest rate) and is usually estimated from historical
6       data, as the slope of the regression of the returns of a stock against the returns of the market
7       over a recently-ended historical period. Estimates based on historical data generally reasonably
8       reflect future expectations, because most companies’ risk profiles change slowly over time.
9       Slowly changing risk profiles prove particularly true for the relatively stable and predictable
10      utility sector.
11          But if a dramatic change in the market or in individual stocks occurs, as in the pandemic-
12      related market turmoil of early 2020, that change will influence the beta estimate for as long
13      as the period of change is included in the trailing data used in the beta calculation, even if
14      investors’ risk perceptions have returned to their level prior to the dramatic change. Analysts
15      should always examine whether the change in market conditions was temporary or is sustained.
16      Mr. Coyle’s analysis suffers from his failure to examine whether the pandemic-related change
17      in market conditions was temporary or has been sustained.
18   Q. HOW CAN WE DETERMINE WHETHER THE CHANGE IN INVESTORS’ RISK
19      PERCEPTIONS WAS TEMPORARY OR HAS BEEN SUSTAINED?
20   A. Determining whether the change in investors’ risk perception was temporary or has been
21      sustained is typically done by examining how betas calculated using different amounts of
22      trailing data and returns calculated at different frequencies – for example, daily, weekly, or
23      monthly – have changed over time.
24   Q. IS THE NEED TO ESTIMATE BETA USING DIFFERENT METHODOLOGIES
25      WELL KNOWN?
26   A. Yes. Utility cost of capital expert witnesses Michael Vilbert and Bente Villadsen have written
27      about the trade-offs of different methodologies, highlighting the need to consider shorter
28      calculation intervals in the wake of abrupt disruptions such as was experienced first during and
29      then immediately after the pandemic-driven bout of market turmoil in early 2020:


                                    Justin Barnes Direct Testimony, on behalf of GIPL
                                                GPSC Docket No. 44280
                                                         Page 58

                                  PUBLIC DISCLSOURE VERSION


 1                        The choices for the interval for the return data and the length of
 2                        the beta estimation window involve trade-offs between
 3                        obtaining more observations through the choice of a longer
 4                        window and/or more frequent return data, ensuring that no
 5                        structural change has occurred during the estimation window,
 6                        and avoiding problems due to insufficient trading activity. …
 7                        Balancing these considerations, economists typically
 8                        recommend estimating beta using daily, weekly, or monthly
 9                        returns over the most recent 2- to 5-year period, with weekly
10                        being the more common, except if there are reasons to think that
11                        the industry might be subject to recent changes in systematic risk
12                        so that the use of a more recent data window is desirable. 111


13            The need to examine beta using different calculation methodologies is also reflected in data
14         providers’ offerings. As explained previously, Bloomberg allows users to easily override its
15         default beta calculation parameters. S&P GMI, in addition to reporting betas calculated using
16         1 and 3 years of trailing data, provides its users with spreadsheet models that allow them to
17         modify all of its beta calculation parameters.
18            In using both Value and Bloomberg betas, Mr. Coyne implicitly acknowledges that no
19         single beta calculation methodology necessarily reflects current investor expectations. But the
20         differences in the Value Line and (modified) Bloomberg beta methodologies he uses are
21         immaterial. Their different market indexes – NYSE Composite for Value Line, S&P 500 for
22         Bloomberg – are nearly perfectly correlated (0.96 correlation 112), and their slightly different
23         Blume adjustment weights yield differences in beta of 2% or less across the range of typical
24         raw utility betas (0.4-1.0). Mr. Coyne’s chosen methodologies hardly reflect the wide range of
25         ways beta could be calculated, each of which could produce dramatically different results. As
26         Nobel laureate Fischer Black, one of the pioneers of empirical testing of beta and the CAPM,
27         famously admonished, “Watch out for data mining!” 113 – running an analysis several different
28         ways but reporting only the outcomes that support one’s conclusions.
